items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: So not only have there b een only five cases brought
by Labour members of Parliament to the Earthq uake Commission in the last 3 years but
two of them have been brought to the co mmission by Poto Williams, who has been in
the place for only 6 months. So what we sa w the other day was the most despicable
political manipulation of a vulnerable person in Canterbury. Did they  tell us when they
found out that that poor woman was in that  bad circumstance? No. They went and
organised a photo opportunity for David Cun liffe and Clayton Cosgrove and Ms Dyson
to turn up there and grandstand on the misery of that woman. That is utterly despicable
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16271
and it is typical of the way Labour members ha ve behaved in Christchurch for the last
3½ years—utterly, utterly despicable behaviour.
The comments about the size of the Cant erbury Earthquake Recovery Authority I
find quite amusing. Firstly, it was never meant to be just a small policy shop. There was
a massive gap in the capability of the Ch ristchurch City Counc il to deliver on any
recovery plans. So I would simply ask La bour members this: tell us what work the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority  should stop—tell us what work the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority should stop. And what do we get? Blank
faces and more ranting—blank faces and more ranting. Just tell us one thing that the
authority should not be doing.
There has been a huge job done in Canter bury by the workers who are part of the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority. There are some 24 recovery plans in place.
The Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authorit y leads 14 of those. It sits alongside
community organisations that lead others. There has been a massive effort to re-zone
land and to make it safe for people to occ upy. Yes, I have to say it is disappointing—
again that word—because things could have gone more quickly. But the courts have had
far too much to say, in my opinion, and ha ve, in fact, not understood what natural
justice is for people who are waiting even now to fi nd out what they are doing.
[Interruption] Now you see the sort of reaction that is being exhibited over there—
ranting, screaming, raging, mock anger. Th at does not do anythi ng for anyone who has
got a difficult circumstance to deal with.
I say again that I have got  the evidence here and I am going to table it—only five
complaints to the Earthquake Commission by Labour Party members. There were two
from Ms Dyson, one from Ms Dalziel, and tw o from Poto Williams, who, to her credit,
in only 6 months has managed to get those complaints up. It wa s a shocker the other
day. To use that 85-year-old woman in the way the Labour Party did was simply
outrageous. There was not a darned thing that the photo opportu nity with David
Cunliffe could achieve—nothing. And did they  tell us how long they had known it? I
understand they knew for 3 months. They knew before Christmas that that woman was
living in those disastrous circumstances. Did they tell us? No, they sat on it because this
was an opportunity for David to come down and do some big grandstanding over this.
I am going to seek another speaking slot [Bell rung]. Mr Chairman?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The Hon Gerry Brownlee.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: There are over 55,000 damaged homes that have now
been completed through the Earthquake  Commission’s earthquake recovery
programme. I take the Committee back to just  immediately after these disasters, when
there were three important things that were said to us. Those things were, firstly, that
our population would fall and start to leave the city; secondly, that real estate values
would fall dramatically and pe rhaps take up to a decade a nd a half to recover; and,
thirdly, that we would have widespread unemp loyment and other social deprivation that
is typical of disasters around the world. Part ly because of the Government’s response,
but mostly because of Cantabrians’ response to what the Government has done in this
process, we do not have any of  those statistics f acing us at the present time. We have
got a growing population in Canterbury. We have in Canterbury the lowest
unemployment of anywhere in New Zealand, and we have real estate prices rising to a
point where some would say it is now a problem.
The one thing that is absolutely certain is  that if people are to live good lives, they
need to have income. The Government move d very quickly after the earthquakes to put
in place the wage subsidy—an amount that meant that any employer could claim up to
$500 per worker per week while that business was reorganising itself to get back on its
feet. That held employment in Canterbury. It gave time for businesses to move into new
16272 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
premises and to relocate in or der to offer their services or their products, or whatever it
might have been. The consequence of that is that we have had record levels of exports
out of Canterbury over the last four or five  quarters, and we have an economy that is
now growing at close to 7 percent. All a ugurs well for the future of Canterbury. The
remaining Earthquake Commissi on properties that are still problematic ar e, in fact,
mostly multiple units—there may be up to, in one case, 43 units on one title—with a
range of insurers all trying to work out who pa ys for what. In the future we will have to
look at land tenure, we will have to look at  conveyancing rules, and we will have to
look at the way in which bodies corporate are required to operate in order to ensure this
disaster does not happen anywhere else in New Zealand.
To suggest that there is total doom and gloom  in Canterbury is quite wrong. There is
despair at the inability—it would seem after 5 months—of the new council to get on top
of its bureaucracy. I say again to Labour me mbers that if there is anything they can
definitely demonstrate that the Canterbur y Earthquake Recovery Authority should not
be doing, then I want to know about it, becau se I cannot think of one thing it is doing
that is a duplication of council efforts or a duplication of any other efforts. I can think of
a lot of well-meaning NGOs that want to be doing more in this space, but the reality is
that there has to be the resource available.  This Government has not been stinting in
making money and resource available to move things forward.
I would like to take time, if it was availa ble, to talk about some of the Earthquake
Commission cases that have made their way in to the media in recent times. I would like
to talk about some of the Southern Respons e cases that have made their way into the
media in recent times. All I would say is th at if people want to go to the media and
complain that they are not being fairly treated, they have an obligation to put all of the
information on the table so that everyone can see exactly how they are being treated. I
suggest there would be many throughout New Zealand who might struggle to
understand that there was mistre atment involved in many of t hose cases. It is a big job,
and no one is resiling from that. It is a big job for the insure rs. It is a big job for the
Earthquake Commission.
One thing that I must comment on is a Marsh report just recently saying that private
insurers in Canterbury have performed worse than in many other disasters in the world.
The subtle difference, but the extremely impor tant difference, is that we had 21 months
of shakes before we got a 3-month period when the insurers could start their work.
Further to that, we have got a penetration rate of insuranc e in New Zealand of over 98
percent. No other jurisdiction in the world ha s that level. So, yes, it might be easy to
say: “Oh well, the insurers ha ve done their work somewhere else.” The fact is they had
a lot fewer insured.
Report noted.
Ministry of Transport

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: If we had had more oppor tunity, I think we should
have had a closer look at  the Ministry of Transpor t and its Turnaround Plan for
KiwiRail, because clearly the Government’s  commitment to turning round KiwiRail is
coming off the tracks, as we have seen in th e past few days. In fact, there has been a
litany of problems over the last year or s o. We have seen the imported Chinese wagons.
The locomotives are having to have their br akes completely replaced, and now we have
asbestos in the locomotives. I will get back to that in a minute. We have seen the
debacle with Peruvian sleepers, which are having to be replaced by contractors right
throughout the country. I am told that some of those sleepers are still so dangerous that
railway workers cannot walk on them.
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16273
We have seen the issue in the Kaimai Tunnel last year, wher e contractors were
exposed to unnecessary and unhealthy gas risks.  That was all to do with contractors and
the fact that they were not carrying out thei r health and safety requirements. We have
had the debacle with the Aratere ferry. There has just been a catalogue of problems, and
I say that this goes back to the Turnaround Plan and the approach of this Government of
cost cutting, of lowest-cost tendering, of contracting out, and of putting pressure on our
national railway to deliver profits on freight while cutting costs everywhere else—while
cutting costs everywhere else.
Here we are today, and that approach is now  putting workers’ lives at risk. That is
where we have ended up. We have asbestos in these locomotives. We have a rolled-over
locomotive in Auckland on which work has now been stopped. The only reason that the
workers did not carry on driving those loco motives was that the unions said that, no,
workers were not going to put their lives on  the line for this killer—killer—asbestos.
The unions said they were not going to allow their workers to be exposed to that.
I understand—and I would challenge the Mini ster of Transport to tell me I am
wrong—that there was real reluctance from  KiwiRail to stop t hose trains, those
locomotives, being used. It was proposing, actu ally, that they coul d keep driving them,
that it was safe, and that they could be contained. We are talking, as I said, about a killer
substance. It is amazing to me and many other people who have been across this story in
the last few days that we still import asbestos into New Zealand. It is still legal to do so.
Even though the Chinese company gave com mitments that there was no asbestos in
the trains, the warning signs have been ther e for some time. Over last November the
Australians found asbestos in Chinese-made  locomotives. The warning sign was there.
KiwiRail checked it and came back and said there was none. Well, of course there was.
So I put the blame squarely on this Mini ster of Transport and on the KiwiRail
Turnaround Plan, which he is responsible for.  He has a lot of que stions to answer. I
want to know when he knew that there was as bestos in these locomotives. When did he
find out?
I happen to know that Kiwi Rail found out about this la st Wednesday—that is, 25
February. KiwiRail did not te ll the workers until the 28 th, 3 days later, and did not tell
the public until Saturday. I want to know from the Minister of Transport whether he was
involved in conversations with KiwiRail at th at time about whether it should go public
and whether it should try to persuade thos e workers to continue to work on those
locomotives. The thing about railway workers is  that their history with asbestos goes
back a long, long way. They have fought this for years and years and years. So it is
completely understandable that they are horrified. They are afraid of the exposure they
have had.
I think the bottom line of all of  this that gets to me is that this Government and the
Minister made the decision with the Turnar ound Plan to have th ese locomotives and
wagons and other things made in China. We lost an entire workshop and skilled workers
because of it. Here we are now, at the end of  it, with workers’ liv es on the line. I just
find that appalling. I wish the Minister were ab le to get up and take a call in response to
these concerns that we have. I think the thing that we want to see from the Minister and
what we will be seeking—
Report noted.
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Kia ora an ō t ātou. We are talking about the
commerce portfolio, and I want to direct our attention to the need for the Minister of
Commerce to show a greater de gree of commitment to, inte rest in, and ownership of
introducing a way of improving the conduct of  our supermarket sector. I will say
16274 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
nothing about the issues that I am still working on with the Commerce Commission, but
I want this Committee and consumers to know that that was not a consequence of
Minister Loss—Foss—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Gloss.

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: —Gloss. OK, whatever—Hoss. It was not as a consequence
of anything to do with him; it was because s uppliers had raised their concerns with him
and his officials and, in desperation, they raised their concerns with me.
A solution after the Commerce Commission has completed its process—and I do not
want to do anything that impedes that pr ocess—is to establish an adjudicator to
establish a code of conduct that is enfor ceable. There are some models that can be
emulated. I do not think it is a good idea to bring holus-bolus over to New Zealand what
passes in the UK, where there are actually more  operational supermarkets, but there is a
model also in Australia. I will have more to  say in the not too distant future about the
conduct of a certain Australian-owned supermarket in New Zealand and its treatment of
Lotto, but that is another matter.
I think that the Minister needs to be prepared to work collaboratively with this side of
the House, and in particular Clayton Cosgr ove, and take a bipartisan approach. Indeed,
one of the rare sensible things I have hear d from the Green Party that I actually agree
with is that it too not only has a very importa nt part to play but also has already done a
considerable amount of work on a model that can be relied upon to police the corporate
culture, the managerial conduct, and the trea tment not only of th e employees of these
veritable empires but also those people who are seeking to earn a living through the sale
of goods and services to the supermarket em pire. That adjudicator cannot come into
being until there has been a decent review, which I hope will follow after the Commerce
Commission exhaustively goes through the pr ocess and protects the identity and the
investment. I know there are issues of natural justice if serious a nd egregious cases are
referred to them—the supermarket needs to  take responsibilit y—but a review could
actually empower people to hold the supermarkets to a higher level of conduct.
The Woolworths-owned supermarket in New Zealand is accountable to no one. It is
obvious that the chief executive officer doe s not know what is going on, and the board
of directors is so distant in Australia, acr oss the Tasman, that it has no genuine idea as
to what is happening here, other than the fact that the supermarket may have been
suffering declining revenues recently. Now th e supermarket is panicking and paying
inordinate amounts of money fo r full-page advertisements, but that is a commercial
decision. The level of interest it is show ing in emblazoning its concerns through an
advertising campaign in the daily newspape rs also needs to be visited upon the
corporate culture and the corporate values that it has engendered in its organisation.
I have indeed been criticised by the Mini ster for being a bit pol emical, but I am not
the architect of the corporate culture that  has fed the concerns that now resonate
throughout the public and occupy the attentio n of the Commerce Commission. It is a
central commerce policy issue. There is an opport unity for that Minister to be bipartisan
and work with our side of the House, in particular Clayton Cosgrove. He has got
experience in these matters. After all, he brought forward a solution to the egregious
conduct that blighted the real estate industr y. So this is a rare opportunity for this
Minister, whose work ethi c could do with a tremendous  degree of growth and
improvement, to work with our side of the House.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia
ora. I rise to take a call on the financial re view of the Ministry of Business, Innovation
and Employment. One department within the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment is energy. What we know when we  look at what the Government is doing
in the energy space is, actuall y, that there is going to be more business, more
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16275
innovation, and more employment when you look at  this side of the House and what its
plans and visions are for energy. Kiwis have a real energy choice this election. On the
one hand, on the blue side, you see a party that is offering New Zealanders more
excuses for rising power prices , a party that is going to be  going to the election with a
track record of power increases of $360 on average, a pa rty that has seen power prices
go up 3 percent despite demand going down 2.5 percent.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Tell us about your carbon tax. How much would carbon tax go up
by?

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Mr Bennett, New Zealanders know all about that sinking
feeling they get when they go to the letterbox  to get a power bill from a big electricity
company under National. What we have seen under the failed National electricity
reforms is that power prices have increas ed 67 percent above inflation since those
Bradford reforms. National is telling New Zealanders their power  prices are not too
high. In fact, they are goi ng to keep going up even when demand is going down.
National is a party that talks about renewables but, in fact, has seen fewer renewables in
New Zealand than we had in 1980 or in 1990.  National is a party that goes around the
country opening gas-fired power stations and sees Huntly extended for another 25 years.
So when that party criticises NZ Power as  seeing more thermal generation, it is very
hollow indeed.
National is a party that is about higher el ectricity prices for Kiwis and less clean
energy for Kiwis, but also Ne w Zealanders’ assets being flogged off. New Zealanders
know all about the Government’s  fiscally reckless, short-si ghted asset sale agenda. We
are losing control of assets , built up over generations of  New Zealanders, for a tiny
amount of money that, in fact, has cost Ki wis, the taxpayers, hundreds of millions of
dollars.
The fourth part of the jigsaw of so -called energy busine ss, innovation, and
employment is deep-sea drilling. Here we have got a sector th at risks hundreds of
thousands of jobs in the rest of the wider economy, a sector that risks a $40 billion cost,
as we saw in the Gulf of Mexico from the very same company that the Government has
invited down to New Zealand—a $40 billion co st. It is an industr y that has got the
lowest job-producing potential of all. So th is election, while National is talking about
excuses for rising prices, assets being flogged off, risky deep-sea drilling, and less clean
energy, the Greens are going to be talking about cleaner, cheaper, smarter power.
The Greens have got a plan, NZ Power, to  deliver $300 a year on average in savings
for Kiwi households. With 42,000 Kiwis disconnected in the last year—four times more
than 5 years ago—it is high time a Governme nt acted to put the interests of New
Zealanders and their power bills before the profits of the big electricity companies. We
have got a plan for 100 percent renewable power. New Zealand can lead the world in
taking action on climate change.
This election we are going to the public sayi ng that although that side of the House
sees excuses, the Green Party will put in sulation under their roofs and will put solar
panels on top. What we know is there is more innovation in terms of the smart grid, and
smart devices on the demand side, powered through NZ Power. We know there are
5,000 jobs, according to Business and Economic Research Ltd, available in NZ Power,
and 1,000 extra jobs when it comes to installing 30,000 solar panels on Kiwis’ roofs. So
when the choice is between a rise in power prices, assets flogged off, and more risky
deep-sea drilling; and, on the other hand, in sulation under your roof and solar panels on
the top—cleaner, cheaper, and smarter pow er—I know what New Zealanders prefer.
This is where the economic benefits for New Zealand are going to come from.
Investment New Zealand says we will ha ve a $150 billion export opportunity in
clean energy and greentech by 2030. We have  got a $6 trillion global market we could
16276 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
be accessing, according to Pure Advant age. PricewaterhouseCoopers, hardly the
Greenpeace of the business world, says there is a $22 billion clean-energy economic
opportunity. Just this week we have seen Bloomberg report record solar installations
around the world. This is growing faster than the oil industry.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a privilege to make  a comment on the report on
the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Em ployment and to talk about productivity,
which is an issue that the ministry ought to be concerned about and have at the front and
centre of its role. It is interesting that in the days past we have been debating publicly
and in this House the issue of KiwiRail a nd the fact that it has locomotives—recently
purchased locomotives—that were made using asbestos. That, in many respects, typifies
the very problem that the New Zealand economy has and that this Government
promotes and perpetuates, time and again, and that is moving down the path of cheap
and nasty. Every opportunity that this Govern ment has to do something, to invest in
New Zealand businesses, to encourage inve stment by New Zealand businesses in their
future and in workers, what does it do? It pl umps for cheap and nast y. It did it with the
locomotives purchased by KiwiRail.
If anybody is under any illusion, let us just unde rstand the risk with asbestos. It takes
only one microscopic fibre to lodge itself in th e lungs of a worker for that worker to be
condemned for life. When they get ill and they  succumb to that single asbestos fibre,
that is it. They have a life of misery until  they die. That is why civilised countries
around the world ban the use of asbestos—Aus tralia has done it for many years—and it
is why it should be the subject of considerable public outrage that we even allow it. The
question, of course, to KiwiRail is where was its procurement manager? Sitting in China
with the manufacturer, providing day-to-day supervision to make sure that the goods we
do not want here were not used in the fabr ication of those locomotives? What was their
approach? Or did we just sort of sign th e order and wait until they came across the
wharves and have them here, causing their problems?
The other issue about productiv ity is this. It is a labour market issue. It is an
employment relations issue. If there is one area where this Government is taking us
down the track of cheaper and nastier and wors e and less effective, it is in the area of
employment relations and empl oyment relations law, and our  labour market regulation.
This Government has on its agenda, and is not afraid to introduce it this side of
Christmas and before the election, a set of  laws that will once again deteriorate the
rights of workers and hand even more power to  employers to do what they like. It will
once again dismantle the checks and balances  in the employment relationship that we
have become used to.
Here is the problem we have. We have a dumb enough labour ma rket policy at the
moment, and this Government wants to make  it dumber. We have gone from dumb to
dumber. Our problem is we suffer low pr oductivity in this c ountry. I can tell the
Committee this. It is not an issue about th e quality of our workforce. We have an
outstanding workforce in this country. It is no t the workforce; it is the management, as
attested to by the Productivity Commission in its report that it rel eased around about 23
December last year. It tried to explain a nd account for the difference in productivity
between New Zealand and Australia. The comm ission found that two-thirds of that
productivity difference is not workers, it is not the capital investment, and it is not the
technology we use. It is the quality of our  management. Every time this Government
passes a law like the hated 90-day rule, like abolishing workers’ rights when it comes to
collective bargaining, it hands a licence to our poor-qua lity management to act in even
worse ways and to reduce our productivity even further.
We need a Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment that is on top of those
issues and is giving policy to Government, giving policy to Ministers, that is about
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16277
lifting our performance in th e workplace and when it comes to productivity. We know
the equation when it comes to productivity: if  we want to pay better wages, move
ourselves up the value chain, we have to lift productivity. But everything this
Government is doing—everythi ng that it is doing—is supp ressing the ability and the
potential for this country to improve its productivity performance. It is a disgrace.
Report noted.
Ministry of Justice

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
take a call on this matter. I would like to ta ke the opportunity to th ank the staff of the
Ministry of Justice for the excellent work they have done over the last year, in particular
with the major work of reform that has been  undergone within the ministry, but also in
the provision of justic e generally, the issues that we have around making justice more
accessible, more user-friendly to people, and to demystify many of the things that have
been somewhat mystified over the years.
I would also like to take the opportunity to thank the Justice and Electoral
Committee, which has done sterling work over the last year, and I am sure it will
continue to do so. This is, in  fact, a committee that has worked very hard to come to
consensus opinions wherever it can but also, where it has not been able to have
consensus, it has been able to deal with th e fact that not all pa rties are going to agree
with everything and have done so on a reasonable basis.
One of the areas where the committee ha s been involved and where justice is
obviously involved is that  of electoral reform and electi ons generally. We have seen in
the last year something that we have never seen before in New Zealand, and that is we
have seen a person convicted of electoral fraud in the c ourts. There were 70-odd names
of people, supposedly living at one address, all to do with local government. But if you
think about it now, under the EasyVote card system, which we have been urged by the
Electoral Commission to extend further, 70 of those EasyVote cards would have gone to
one household.
The committee, I know, has been very much involved in looking at how the
EasyVote card could be used, but not to the detriment of the integrity of elections. I
would have thought that anybody who cannot reme mber what their name is as they are
coming up to vote may in fact not be the pe rson whose name is on the EasyVote card. I
would like to thank the committee for its pret ty much, I think, unani mous report back,
which I understand will be deba ted later tonight. But that is some of the work that the
Justice and Electoral Committee doe s, and it is also some of the area of the Ministry of
Justice. The Ministry of Justice ranges right across family law, criminal law, civil law
generally, our human rights r ecord—all those sorts of areas—as well as electoral
reform. It is a huge ministry in terms of its workload, and a huge ministry in terms of
the number of pieces of legislation that it has responsibility for.
Recently I was able to represent New Zealand, along with ministry and other
officials, at the United Nati ons in Geneva on our human ri ghts record, which, I have to
say, was greeted with a tremendous amount of acclaim, frankly. I was really proud to be
representing New Zealand, and I think all members of Parliament should be pleased
with the fact that New Zealand does have an  excellent human rights record, and we will
continue to do so, certainly under this Government.
It was one of the areas where nobody brought  up the electoral issues. They did not
bring up the Electoral Finan ce Act, under a former Government. They did not have to
because we have already dealt with it. They did not have to bring up the foreshore and
seabed legislation, under a former Government, because we have dealt with that too. So
there is a tremendous amount of support.
16278 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
In fact, one of the things that our staff ove r at the ministry were very impressed with
was the number of ambassadors from other co untries who stood in a queue to shake my
hand, on behalf of New Zealand. I have to say I was quite pleased with that. I also felt
that it was a testament to the work of ma ny. It was a testament to the work of this
House, and also a testament to the work of our agencies, which help to keep New
Zealand such a safe and good citizen within the world. As we have seen in Europe
recently—in just the last few days—this is not something that can be taken for granted.
In fact, elections and electoral responsibil ity and integrity are matters that we cannot
take for granted. We cannot presume that  anyone armed with a little card with
someone’s name on it is necessarily the person whom they claim to be. As I have said
before, if you cannot remember what name it is that you are using today, perhaps it is
not you. It is one of the areas where I think we  need to be vigilant. I would like to thank
Denis O’Rourke, whose idea this was in the select committee. I am not sure he is
necessarily supporting it now, but that is called politics. Unfortunately, integrity still has
a way to come within politics. Thank you.
Report noted.
Ministry of Health

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: The health portfolio is in trouble. It
is in serious trouble. After 6 years of Tony Ryall’s stewards hip, 6 years of his decision
making, and 6 years of his policies, he is still blaming the previous Government—and
me in particular, 9 years after I finished being the Minister of Health.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: You made such a mess of it.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: What I want to say to that member opposite, who never
contributes anything in health, is that the blame game is part of his arsenal for managing
health. I want to add to that arsenal the bul lying of chairs and chief executive officers,
of staff and NGOs; controlling the Official Information Act requests that go out and the
information that the Ministry of Health is allowed to put out; and covering up, because I
believe that the Minister of Health knew a lot more about the Sout hern District Health
Board and South Link Health money than he is letting on.
I would give him, under national standard s, an Achieved for politics and a Not
Achieved for making a better health system for New Zealanders, because, in fact, he has
managed to create a climate of fear in the health system of New Zealand. If you want to
look at some of those who work at the coal front who had something to say about this, I
suggest that you read the statement from  the Association of Salaried Medical
Specialists—in other words, our doctors—which  put out a statement last week when it
heard that Mr Ryall is leaving. It said that he is a Minist er of Health with a “mixed
record”, and that it has been “a tale of tw o health ministers”. The statement said: “Tony
Ryall’s performance … got off to a good start but after a c ouple of years his
performance became increasingly disappointing,”. The statement said that he abandoned
“his commitment to address the vulnerability of the hospital specialist workforce”—our
specialist doctors in our hos pitals—by using “dodgy misleading data.” He turned “a
blind eye to public hospitals struggling to function under entrenched specialist
shortages. … Increasingly fi nancially squeezing public ho spitals while increasing the
demands on what they are required to do.” I am  quoting all this from the Association of
Salaried Medical Specialists. He also ha d “Excessive political micro-management,
including threatened financial penalties,”.  He created a “punitive culture in public
hospitals”, and there was a “failure to invest in the health workforce in public hospitals,
including senior doctors,”.
That came from our senior doctors working in the health system. Those are not my
words; they are their words. In fact, his in sidious and bullying approach to the portfolio
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16279
has now led to staff being afraid to speak out, being scared that their jobs will be at risk,
and being unable to give free and frank advice.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: It’s not doing you any good, Annette.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: It has led to NGOs and provide rs being scared that their
funding will not continue if they do not agree with the Mini ster. So I say to the member
who is over there interjecting, let me read to her a very unusual letter I have received: “I
am a long-time loyal employee of the Ministry of Health. I have worked in the sector
for many years. I cannot recall a time when the targeting has become so personalised
and insidious, and it has been dangerous to wo rk in the health sector. There appears to
be overt targeting of both chairs and chief executive officers in a number of district
health boards. It is embarrassing to s ee senior leaders bully ing, dominating, and
shouting at individual di strict health boards. Increasingl y, district health boards are
required to have all of their Official Information Act requests checked and agreed to, to
ensure that the messages are controlled and the information modified. Increasingly the
messages are verbal, so nothing can be traced. There is no sense of direction and the
leadership is totally inept. District hea lth boards are overtly being disempowered and
made ineffective. There is no understanding in  the sector. This is an increasing risk to
health.”
Those words come from those working in th e health sector, and that is why I think
that they need to be exposed, because this Minister has been very successful in keeping
the lid on health but not successful in im proving the health of many New Zealanders.
We have learnt in these last few days the cost of going to a doctor for adult New
Zealanders has gone up.
Report noted.
Ministry of Education

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I am very pleased to take a call on the
financial review of the Ministry of Education. First of all, I want to begin by addressing
my comments to all of those teachers up and down the country who are continuing to
experience the poor effects of the Novopay pa yroll system. A year and a half after
Novopay was implemented we still have a syst em that is not paying people what they
are owed. It is still a system in which school principals and administrators are having to
spend hours and hours and hours every pay cycl e sorting out problems or finding ways
around problems. I think that is completely  unacceptable. The Government put Steven
Joyce in charge of Novopay a year ago to fix it, and he has failed to do so. Instead, what
we have seen is a gloss of paint slapped over the top of it and St even Joyce saying we
have dealt with all of the pr oblems and things are getting better. They are not getting
better. Schools are still consumed by Novopay problems, and the Government is simply
turning a deaf ear to those problems. That is not good enough. It is time for Novopay to
be scrapped so that schools can get on with the job of teaching and learning and not be
constantly distracted by having to deal with payroll issues.
Teachers work incredibly hard. We value the work of teachers. We value the work of
school support staff—that is everyone from  the teacher aides through to cleaners,
caretakers, school administrators, librarians. Th ey all work very hard for the benefit of
our education system. They deserve to be paid  what they are owed. They deserve to be
able to rely on the fact that their pay pack et will be in their bank account each fortnight.
At the moment they cannot have that reassu rance. It is a year and a half now since
Novopay was implemented. It is still not workin g. That is simply not good enough. It is
time for the Government to actually step up and say that if Novopay cannot deliver—
and clearly it cannot—it is time to pull the pin on it and put in place a system that
works, because this has gone on for long enough.
16280 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
Moving on, I want to talk about  a couple of other issues that were raised during the
financial review process. The first is the introduction of partnership schools, because, of
course, more information has become appare nt since the financial review into the
Ministry of Education took place. It has now become apparent, for example, that
partnership schools are receivi ng up to five times the aver age funding of State schools.
That is clearly wrong. The Government, of course, is trying to load the deck in favour of
partnership schools succeeding, but if every other school in the country was given a
level of funding equivalent to what is being given to partnership schools, I am sure that
they would be doing a lot better as well.
This is a Government committed to creating a two-tier education system: a small
minority who will do very well out of it, and th e vast bulk of the rest who will simply
deal with whatever is left over at the e nd of it. That is not good enough. Our focus has
to be on making sure that every school in New Zealand is a great school and that every
teacher is a great teacher. I do not think we should be creating a two-tier teaching
profession and I do not think that we shoul d be creating a two-tier schooling system,
and, unfortunately, many of the policies of this Government go in exactly that direction.
We should be focused on making sure that  every child in New Zealand has the
opportunity to reach their full potential, an d that means we have to recognise the
enormous work that is done by the dedica ted and committed group of teachers that we
have in our classrooms already.
I want to say that I am awaiting with interest the outcome of the recent
announcements around the expert teacher posit ions. There are sector working groups
working on that. I have made it very clear that we will wait and see what comes out of
that working group process, be cause if there is broad buy in  and support for some of
those roles from within the sector, then we will support those, as we ll. I have got real
reservations about some of those roles that  have been announced, but we will await the
outcome of that process before we make any further announcements on that.
What is very clear, however, is that the lack  of trust that exists within the education
system at the moment will be one of the biggest impediments to any change being
successful. People simply do not trust that  the current Govern ment is going to
implement this new system in a way th at will be respectable of the teaching
profession—that will genuinely embrace th e nature of a strongly collegial and
collaborative teaching profession, an aut onomous teaching profession. People do not
trust that the Government is  actually going to deliver on those things, so although they
may think that there are elements of the prop osals that they also agree with, they are
very, very reluctant to sign up to this packag e, because they simply do not have trust in
the current Government to deliver on it. That is true right across the board in education,
and that has got to be addressed.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. There are so many issues inside
education funding that it is very difficult to contain oneself to a si ngle topic, or to be
contained to only 5 minutes. I could, for exam ple, point to what is an obvious ploy of
the National Government of announcing headlin e-grabbing budget lines in one Budget,
taking a month’s worth of media coverage on that budget line, then quietly removing
that same budget unspent in the following year, and then usi ng the same bookwork
transaction to give itself another headline.  I could, for example, point to the National
Government’s lauding of its investment into education. It is going into this election
crowing about its increasing sp ending into education. The fact that much of this
spending has nothing to do with a commitment to education but is a requirement due to
a large natural disaster—a requirement to  rebuild the educational facilities of
Christchurch—appears to be lost on its backbe nchers, as is the fact that much of this
spending is required to rebu ild schools throughout New Zealand. It was a National
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16281
Government that changed the building c ode and the building standards and that
approved faulty materials—millions upon millions to fix past National mistakes.
I could warn the New Zealand public about the current trumpeting by this
Government of its supposed increased inve stment in education from the Budget under
discussion to the more recent Budgets. I could warn the New Zealand public that when
the Government says th at it is investing more than ever  before in education, it does not
mean this to futureproof the public education system; rather, it is fattening the goose for
sale. National is implementing a marketable  business model over ou r public schools so
that, should it successfully gain a third term in Government, it will extend the partial
privatisation via charter sc hools to all New Zealand sc hools, as was previously
advanced by this party in the 1990s.
But I will have to content myself with  a single piece of propaganda from this
Government, directly from this Budget. Th is single example shows how the National
Government’s policy of “plug and play” when it comes to Ministers, which leads to a
reliance on officials’ high-level thinki ng, which in turn leads to unintended
consequences, impacts negatively on the childr en of New Zealand. I refer to the Budget
announcement on increases to the early childhood education equity funding—the

items.speaker: Budget announcement that said
items.text: “$47.9 million is  being invested over 4 years in Equity
Funding to support learners in our target comm unities.” What were the targets for this
supposedly additional funding? They were to be: “A. Low socio-economic community”,
“B. Special needs and non-English speak ing background”, “C. Language and culture
other than English”, and “D. Isolation.” The Ministry of Education and the Minister of

items.speaker: Education made the following statement
items.text: “We e xpect that services that receive Equity
Funding will use the increased funding to in crease the enrolment and participation of
children from the priority groups by taking actions such as: keeping ECE fees low so
children from priority families can support and maintain regular participation,
encouraging and supporting family/wh ānau to actively engage and support what their
children are learning … provide additiona l resourcing for learning in te reo M āori and
Pasifika languages.”
So how has that worked out for New Zeal and? Well, let us talk about the New
Zealand Playcentre Federation, an organi sation internationally recognised, an
organisation that goes directly  to low early childhood educa tion costs with the direct
involvement of wh ānau and family, and, even more th an that, an organisation that
provides opportunities for those family members,  those parents, to gain education at no
cost. Well, as we debate this Budget, Pl aycentre is nationally in crisis. Unless the
current funding context changes, then at l east 483 playcentres acr oss New Zealand will
continue to crumble and they will close. Playcentre’s only hope is to hold on long
enough for a change of Government later this year.
How about mobile kindergarten s? How about the killing off of Hunterville’s mobile
kindergarten through Government funding cu ts and increased compliance? Mobile
kindergartens involve teachers tr avelling to a number of rural or isolated areas with a
range of equipment and resources and runni ng kindergarten sessions for young children
and their families. They provide early chil dhood education services in areas in which
few other early childhood education services ar e available. Who will fill this gap? They
will close. They are about to close, running at a $100,000 loss because the funding
model no longer fits. Who will f ill that gap for our rural children? Private business? Do
not be ridiculous. There are not enough numbers  to provide the comm ercial viability of
a business to go into these areas, but that  does not minimise the Government’s
responsibility to rural communitie s for their children to be ab le to access these services
inside marae, inside community halls.
16282 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: T ēnā koutou e te Whare nui o te Whare
Pāremata. Tēnā koutou katoa. I am pleased to take a call on Vote Education, although it
saddens me because the education space shoul d be a manifestation of harmony for the
benefit of all our children’s learning, instead of which it is now a highly contested space
between those who seek to privatise and t hose who want quality local public education,
which includes innovation, to be the priorit y. That is what we have been struggling
with, I guess, under Vote Education for the last couple of years.
We need foreign charter school s like a fish needs a bicycle. We need privatisation in
the same way that we need the aforementioned bicycle. We actually need to think about
what the public-private partnerships that ha ve just been announced by the Minister of
Education today will do to the quality public education system, which we are trying to
strengthen. It is very interesting to see the cost-cutting and the property speak in the
Cabinet paper that I have just been trying to read, which shows that schools are going to
be “bundled together”—I love the rhetoric here—to see whether there is money to be
made out of them under the name of relie ving teachers and principles from managing
school property.
Well, if one has read any of the international literature on public-private partnerships,
the contract still has to be managed by the sc hool. Schools have to deal with the private
company that is making the money—or not—out  of the school, and many of them have
been left holding the baby. That is very, ve ry worrying when we see the master plan for
privatisation that has been rolled out this afternoon in this country.
Christchurch, of course, is the Trojan Horse for all of this. I was there last week and
one of the principals said to me that it ta kes him far more time to manage his school
cleaning contractor than it does to have pe ople work for him directly. He said that
managing contracts is actually far more time- consuming and difficult  than just dealing
with the people whom he knows who used to come in and clean his school. That was a
minor example of his concerns about public-p rivate partnerships, about which he knew
nothing. He is from east Christchurch a nd is very intimatel y involved—supposedly
involved—in the brave new world that is being created in the modern learning
environments.
The other thing that was interesting that was said to me was that a modern learning
environment might be some colourful beanbags and some new classrooms, but in reality
the community remains the community, with a lack of the resources that they need. He
said: “We as schools are still going to struggle with dealing with what is really going on
with homelessness, with enormous stress,  with poverty, with low wages, and with
families that are under stress.”
So at the heart of the debate, although th e Government will continue to deny this
under Vote Education, is the reality of the child poverty statistics, which the Crown has
admitted have been underestimated by up to more than 20,000 children. That is why we
need to encourage our best people into teaching, and, like others, we watch this space to
see how things play out in terms of the $350 million that has been allocated to give
more money to executive principals and others.
But we also need to acknowle dge that we have to addres s the fundamental issues of
inequality, and the Green Party has done s o. The Green Party has developed a package
on the hearts and hubs of co mmunities, how schools can be better at meeting those
needs, open our doors, and be dedicated communities. There is a huge and ironic
difference between the idea of a public-private  partnership with services managed by a
manager to make sure they are efficient and the idea in the Greens package of dedicated
school coordinators to organise programmes with communities.
That could be Te Reo M āori, it could be a dult and community education, it could be
language classes, it could be social workers, it could be dental health, it could be
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16283
parenting programmes, it could be whatever th e community wants, not to see whether it
is more efficient, whether more money can  be made, and whether the Government can
cut its spending on property, but to build communities. Free after-school and holiday
programmes for children in decile 1 to 4 schools, a school nurse in those schools, and
lunch for those decile 1 to 4 sc hools, if they want it, based on how they want to deliver
it—all of these can be done and we have costed them for under $88 million per annum.
And we have received very positive fee dback from educators and communities about
this package. We think it is a far better i nvestment than investigating privatisation of
school property or paying executive princi pals, who have got to look after 10 other
schools and mentor them 2 days a week while running their own schools.
We think ours is a better investment. It is the difference between shallow and deep
support for schools and communities in the reality that we face. Principals of low-decile
schools tell me that low-decile environments require a different skill set and a lot more
resources. One example they gave me wa s school support staff. This principal had
taught in both decile 10 and dec ile 1 schools and said that mu ch more needs to be spent
on school support staff in low-decile schools.

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: T ēnā t ātou e te Whare. T ēnā
koutou katoa. I am really pleased to be able to take a call in this financial review debate,
because I would like to take the opportuni ty to publicly commend the Ministry of
Education for the fine work it has been doing in a very ch allenging portfolio. We have
heard from speakers this afternoon, and if we were to believe everyt hing they said, we
would be surrounded by an education syst em characterised by doom and gloom, when,
in fact, out there our schools—over 2,500 schools catering to 832,000 of our 5 to 17 and
18-year-olds—and over 5,000 early childhood edu cation centres of a diverse range of
provision are doing exciting and fulfilling and constructive things.
As Minister of Education I am very relian t on a family of education agencies within
the government sector to undertake that wo rk. The Ministry of Education is key
amongst that. One of the first discussions I had with the new Secretary for Education,
Peter Hughes, was what our particular ro le and contribution w ould be through the
Ministry of Education. A significant change is going on. Whereas once the job of the
Secretary for Education and of the minist ry was characterised as being sector
leadership, what we have recognised very  clearly—unlike previous administrations—is
that the leadership of the sector properly re mains with boards of trustees, our parents
around the country, and the princi pals of those schools. The role of the Ministry of
Education is to provide the systems support to back those schools to be successful in
delivering high-quality teaching and learning so that achievement can rise for all of our
children. And that is what the Ministry of Education is doing.
There is a system change going  on. It is being r ecognised by the sector leaders. That
system change includes changes such as ensu ring that what we are asking of schools
really does add value to their operational environment and is not simply about
compliance. They are appreciating that every fortnight now the Ministry of Education is
communicating with them about the key issues and concerns that they need to be aware
of. They are getting the support from our regi onal offices, which are working with them
on understanding what our invest ment in data means for mo re effective operating of
their schools, but, more properly, on making su re that they are causing learning to
happen and that they know that it is happening.
So I would like to commend the Secretary for Education, his leadership team, and the
ministry as a whole, which is full of very committed people up and down our country
whose job it is to back our 2,500 school s and over 5,000 early childhood education
providers to win. Why? Because we want to be responsive to parents. Whatever
community they come from and whatever le vel of socio-economic status they have,
16284 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
parents want their children to be successful, an d they put a great deal of trust into the
schools and early childhood education providers to ensure that that can be the case. And
there are professionals in school s whose jobs are to make su re that they are able to
deliver their skills, their training, and their expertise to make sure that learning and
engagement are occurring with the young people in front of them and that they are able
to give information to parents in ways th at parents can therefore be empowered to
support their own children’s learning at home and in the community.
We have seen the importance and the necessi ty of ensuring that  parents are being
well supported, and that has led to the transf er of the authority and all of the funding
from the Ministry of Education to the Ne w Zealand School Trustees Association. That
has resulted, in Budget 2013, in an 84 percent increase for the association. It is the
organisation that works with over 16,500 pare nts, relations, and community people who
want to see their school succeeding. We want to  ensure that parents are getting reports
in plain English so that they understand how they can help their children learn, and we
are constantly improving that reporting by ge tting feedback from parents about what
they require. We are investing in a tool k it for parents about the questions they can be
asking their children’s teachers so that they  get the answers that help them to be
informed and helpful towards their children in their learning journey.
The Ministry of Education has been entr usted with $9.7 billion of taxpayers’ money
to bring about a lift in achievement not for th ree out of five of our kids, not for four out
of five, but for every one of our children and young people. We know from the research
that the critical in-school difference is made by the quality of teaching and the quality of
leadership. That saw in January this year th e Prime Minister, in his state of the nation
address, prioritising education and investi ng $359 million in four new roles. Those new
roles will give better career pathways for our  profession and they will support the status
and the profile of the professi on so that we can keep, attrac t, and grow the quality of
teaching and leadership, because in schools that is what makes a difference to
achievement.
And we want to back our profession to win. That is why this Government will be
introducing legislation very shortly to transform the New Zealand Teachers Council into
a 21st century professional  body that is fit for the demands of the 21 st century. That is
why we have invested the $359 million that I ha ve just talked about. That is why we are
hosting education festivals in Auckland, Wellin gton, and Christchurch so that schools
can showcase to each other and to the public a ll of the great things that they are doing
within schools. That is why we have launched an inspiredbyU website, so that each and
every one of us gets the opportunity to thank those teachers who have made a difference
in our lives. That is why New Zealand went in to bat to host the International Summit
on the Teaching Profession.
At the end of March we will be hosting in Parliament nearly 20 Ministers of
Education from around the world, because they want to come to New Zealand to see
what the particular levers are within our system that are making a difference but also
how we can confront together the challenge  that is a challenge to many education
systems, which is how we deliver both excelle nce and equity to all of our children and
young people. Our Ministry of Education, our Vote Education, and this Government are
absolutely committed to backing our system to win and to putting our money where our
mouths are.
Speaking of that money, we are also investing in the platform of schools.
That means school properties, which have been dismissed by previous speakers here.
Modern learning environments really do crea te the context within which these quality
teaching and quality leadership practices can  make magic with ev ery one of our New
Zealand students. Network for Learning, the connecting up of schools to the ultra-fast
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16285
broadband, has been a $700 million investment by this Government, because we know
that the 21 st century demands new ways of lear ning and we want every New Zealand
child to be successful New Zealanders opera ting on a global stage. That is what this
New Zealand education system is committed to.
There was some scaremongering about priva tising our education system. How five
partnership schools out of 2,500 schools can so mehow characterise a privatising agenda
is beyond me, Chicken Licken. The sky has not fallen. What this Government is
prepared to do is trial other al ternatives, invest in other options, to make sure we do get
the five out of five of our young people su cceeding. We cannot keep doing everything
we have always done or we will keep getti ng the results we have always got. Instead,
the result we are getting is a 2.5 percent increase in Nationa l Certificate of Educational
Achievement overall, a 4 percent increase in M āori achievement, and a 7 percent
increase in Pasifika achievement. In term s of getting under-fives  into early childhood
education, we have seen a rise to nearly 96 percent, when our target is 98 percent.
Look, our numbers, our performance, and our  track record speak for itself. The $9.7
billion that has been entrusted into Vote  Education is being spent wisely. That
investment is showing a return. When I use language like that, it is not about
privatising; it is about proving to the taxpaying parents out there that what we are doing
in education is making a difference for each and every child.
Mr Chair, I can and will go on. I will go on an d talk about all the wonderful things
that we are doing across the education system . In terms of early childhood education,
one of the key principles of the New Zealand education system is to provide choice to
parents, whether it is playcentre or kindergarten, whether it is  parent-led or teacher-led,
whether it is home-based or centre-base d. Those choices are one s that we profoundly
believe parents in New Zealand have the righ t to make on behalf of  their children for
what they think is the best learning opportuni ty. That is equally true of our formal and
compulsory education system. We have small rural schools. We have large metropolitan
schools. We have faith-based schools. We ha ve coed schools. All of these choices are
available to our parents so that their childr en can have the education they deserve to
create the best possible New Zealand we can have.

Vote Treaty Negotiations, Non-departmental appropriations
Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON (Minister for Treaty of Waitangi
Negotiations): This is such an important area th at I think a brief statement by me on
where we are at and how we are going is appr opriate. I am disappointed that the Labour
Party has not chosen to speak a bout this area, because it is so critically important. I am
very proud of the Office of Treaty Settlements  and the outstanding work that has been
done by its very dedicated ba nd of highly qualified and utterly professional civil
servants. They are an outstanding bunch of  people, ably assisted by some excellent
Crown negotiators. The Crow n negotiators, who number among them people like the
Hon Paul Swain, the former Labour MP for Rimutaka, who is the chair of the Crown
negotiators, do a wonderful job indeed. Th ere is the former Labour member of
Parliament for Tukituki Rick Barker, who has been doing some tremendous work for
me up in Taranaki. There is John Wood, a former twice-appointed New Zealand
Ambassador to Washington, who was res ponsible for negotiating the great and
historical settlement with Ng āi T ūhoe and who has also been doing some tremendous
16286 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
work on the Whanganui River. So there are some really fine people who have been
working with the Office of Treaty Settlements,  and the reality is th at they have made
excellent progress in the last few years.
I was so proud to be with some of my pa rliamentary colleagues signing a deed of
settlement with Ng āti Kur ī. I want to also mention Pat Snedden, who did some
wonderful work with the Te Hiku Forum iwi.  I wondered whether we would ever get to
the stage where we signed deeds of settlement in the far north, but we did. Four of the
five Te Hiku Forum iwi have now signed deed s of settlement, and I believe that those
iwi and that area will go from strength to strength.
As we come down the country, I, of course, have to mention the work that has been
done by the Office of Treat y Settlements on the Ng āpuhi mandate. That really has been
something in the nature of a Homeric epic. A couple of weeks ago I delivered to both
factions the decision that we have made on the mandate. I really do endorse what the
Hon Shane Jones has been saying in public that now is the time for the Ngāpuhi factions
to come together for the negotiation, to see what they can do to get a good settlement,
because one reads in the New Zealand Herald, for example, stories about the economic
suffering in places like Kaikohe. Now is the time  to negotiate a settlement so that those
sorts of communities in the north can benef it economically and also socially, and they
should talk to their wh ānau in the Te Hiku Forum iwi because they can see what can be
achieved when you work together for a common aim.
I am very pleased with what is being done in T āmaki and Hauraki. They are very
complex negotiations. Of course, the House will soon be debating the Tāmaki collective
legislation. Michael Dreaver, an outstanding Treaty negotia tor, has been doing great
work in T āmaki and down into Hauraki, and I hope that before the end of the year we
will have deeds of settlement with at leas t 11 of the 12 Hauraki iwi as well as two
settlements with the Marutūahu collective and with the Hauraki collective.
I am so very pleased with the work that has been done in Taranaki. Again I have
referred to the work of Rick Barker and Paul  Swain. This really is bipartisan work. I
have got those guys involved since they have left Parliament, and they have done a great
job working with Te Ātiawa, Ngā Ruahine, and Taranaki. When those deeds are signed,
that will leave Ngāti Maru and the collective settlement for that province, and that really
is good.
I know that the member for Ikaroa-R āwhiti will have more than a passing interest
down the East Coast. Great work is being done  with discussions with Te Tira, He Toa
Takitini in Hastings, Rangit āne ki Wairarapa, and now with Ng āti Kahungunu ki
Wairarapa. So there is a lot of work going on down there, and I would hope that in the
very near future we are going to have some full and final settlements.
So this is very important work. We know  that we are not dealing with full
compensation, but Treaty settlements are abou t more than money. They do provide iwi
with a strong economic base, but, importa ntly, they deal with acknowledging the
historical wrongs, making that apology, and, as we see for example with Ng āti Whare,
we deal with social accords as well. A town that really was the victim of the 1980s
extremist policies of the Labour Government, a town that suffered greatly, was a town
called Minginui. It always amuses me to hear the Labour Party members talk about
poverty when for 9 years they did nothing about Minginui. I am  on a steering group
with the Mayor of Whakatāne and numerous others dealing with—
