Ministry of Social Development

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to take a short call on the
estimates for social services. I think it is ap propriate that we reflect on recent events in
this portfolio. For the last few months the Government has been claiming that it has
made progress on key indicators. When I say “key indicators”, I do not actually mean
child poverty necessarily, because the Government has chosen not to make that a Public
Service target. No, child poverty has not be en imbedded within the Government’s key
goals for this portfolio. Inst ead, it has decided to pick o ff things like immunisation,
insulation of housing, and so on.
No one is denying that they are important areas where we would like to see gains, but
it would be disingenuous to suggest that an y of those do anythi ng to make a nudge,
make a dent, in the core issue of child poverty itself. But even then, even though it is not
a key goal of the Government to reduce child poverty, it has still made a claim—in fact,
the Minister of Finance made the claim in th e chair today—that that has been one of the
key focuses of this Government. So says the Government that has spent probably the
most substantive Government spend on tax br eaks, which did not positively affect those
families. That Minister still tried to claim that at the fore of his thinking was child
poverty and income inadequacy. How can that be? Where have we seen a dent in child
poverty figures? The reality is that we have not.
If you ask the Government what it has done on child poverty, the one thing it
continues to raise is that it is focused on moving people from benefits into work. Well,
that completely ignores the fact that two out of five of the children living in poverty—
and that is probably likely to change based on the recalculations that are happening as
we speak—are in the homes of the working poor. They are in families where the parents
are fulfilling the social contract of old: if you work a 40-hour week, you can provide for
your family. It is not so. It is not so under this Government.
We have a new class of working poor. The Government refuses—refuses—to
address income inadequacy, and as long as it does, it will not make a dent in our child
poverty statistics. In fact, we know that the statistics are actually worse than we first
thought. For a long time now, we have been ashamed at the fact that we have 265,000
children living in poverty. We now know, as  of a week ago, that we have 285,000
children in poverty. That is 27 percent of children in New Zealand. How do we know?
Well, we know that Treasury made a mist ake. It double-counted  the accommodation
supplement. There are more families worse off than we first thought.
But, actually, there is another devastating statistic that we ha ve not placed enough
emphasis on. There is an increase in the num ber of families who are living on not 60
percent of the median household income, whic h is the general measure we tend to use,
but on 50 percent or less. That means the number of families living in severe poverty
has increased from 12 percent to 14 percent. That is something that all of us should be
worried about.
What is the Government’s reaction to that ? Well, actually, the Government has said
that even then, even th ough there are 20,000 more children in poverty than it first
thought, it has still made good progress because it is fewer than in 2010 when we
reached a ridiculous high of 300,000 childre n in poverty—another new statistic based
on the recalculation. So, apparently, we s hould celebrate that we have gone from
absolutely dismal ridiculous failure to shamef ul failure. There is nothing to celebrate in
any of those statistics.
The fact remains that still not enough is  being done by this Government to move
away from the in-kind assistance that it has focused on and towards addressing systemic
change. Everything that the Government has put  out to try to step away from the fact
that we have this now higher and more sham eful child poverty sta tistic has been about
16288 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014

items.speaker: Working for Families. Government members say
items.text: “Look, we’ve got Working for
Families. That’s cushioned the recession.”, a nd, secondly, “All this does is prove that
the recession was worse than we thought.” We ll, I would like to challenge that. No one
is doubting that the recession had an economic impact. No one is questioning that. But
also, on this side of the Hous e, our argument has been that it was in the Government’s
power to do something that would actually change that, and it did not.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: There are 285,000 child ren in this country  living in poverty.
That is because of this G overnment’s decisions. That number boggles my mind. I grew
up in a city of around 45,000 peopl e. To think that six cities ’ worth of children in this
country are now living without th e basics offends me at a very deep level. About one in
four of our children are now  living in poverty. They are our children, and their poverty
is our poverty. As already mentioned, two out of five of these children have parents who
are working. To quote—as has been quoted many times in the last year or so in this
House—the words of Nelson Mandela: “Overcom ing poverty is not a ta sk of charity; it
is an act of justice. Like slavery and aparth eid, poverty is not natu ral. It is man-made
and it can be overcome and eradicated by the actions of human beings.”—that is, by the
actions of the Government, its policies a nd budgets; policies and budgets that we have
not seen from this Government.
This Government has chosen not to m easure poverty. It has knowingly hidden the
real levels of poverty from us while it happily  used figures that it  knew were incorrect
to justify its performance. Today in this Co mmittee it has listed off all the money it is
spending on these children—these  lucky children—and told us  that the Salvation Army
has suggested that the Government spend less on children. That is disingenuous and,
frankly, offensive. This Government has ta ken $1.1 billion a year from all of us and
given it to the top 10 percent of income earners. That is $1.1 billion a year it could have
used to reduce poverty, to feed our kids and ma ke sure that they are warm and healthy.
The 285,000 children without the basics cannot be dismissed with misinformation.
Under this Government, ther e are 45,000 more children li ving in poverty than when
this Government came to power. That is an entire city’s worth of children without
enough. This Government has told us child povert y is a problem of the parents. Then it
has told us the country cannot afford to pay fa mily carers a legal wage. It has told us it
cannot afford to extend paid pare ntal leave. It has told the co urts that rest homes should
not be required to pay women equal pay for work of equal value.  It has reduced the
bargaining powers of workers. It has made it more difficult to get disability support. It is
not informing beneficiaries of their protecti ons and entitlements. How can parents help
their children when this Government is cr eating barriers to the basic entitlements and
undermining the ability of those in work to look after themselves and their children?
I hear from far too many sole parents that they are trying to l ook after their children
but feel ashamed for not being in paid wor k. I have heard of pare nts having to choose
between buying medication for their children and food, and worrying that if they choose
food, then there may be a notification to Child , Youth and Family for neglect. That is
the level of pain that this Government is re sponsible for, and it is not the vision of an
inclusive society that this country was built on.
Children have told us directly that they re ally worry when their parents are stressing
out about not having enough money, and school lunches are not going to solve that.
Children have told us that they think that this Government is gi ving money to the rich
people and that those rich people are spending it on things they do not need. We need to
listen to the wisdom of our children. Poverty may feel in exorable to those burdened by
it but the truth is that we can reduce it. It is a matter of values.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: I would like to start my contribution by talking about
what Miss Ardern talked about. She seemed to discount the fact that immunisation for
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16289
our children is important and that home insulation is important. These are very
important factors. These are the deliverables that we have delivered as a Government.
As Parliamentary Private Secretary to the Minister for Ethnic Affairs I am often
meeting dignitaries from many  different countries who visit our shores, and often their
conversations turn to compliments about Ne w Zealand and how New Zealand is in an
enviable position with our economic outlook, even with the devastating earthquakes that
Canterbury has gone through. New Zealand is, in fact, on track  to deliver a surplus in
2014-15, when most other countries are in deficit. What this means is that we start to
pay off our debt. What the Opposition member s do not seem to understand is that when
they borrow the money to pay people, whatever they actually promise, they are putting
our future and the future of our children a nd our grandchildren in debt for a very, very
long time.
More jobs have been created. Seventeen thousand fewer people were on a benefit in
December 2013 compared with the year befo re. There are 12,000 fewer kids in benefit-
dependent homes than there were in December 2012. Long-term welfare dependency is
falling, and we are continuing to help familie s and older New Zealanders with income
support. In the past year this Government helped 80,000 people off welfare and into
work. Paid work is the best route out of hardship for families who are finding it difficult
to make ends meet. I remember a saying that is something like this: give a man a fish
and it will feed him for a day, but when you teach the man how to fish, it will feed him
for a lifetime. When you just give him a handout, he may be able to feed himself and his
family for a day, but when you actually teach him to work and go and find a job, he
might be able to provide for himself and his family for the rest of his life.
There was an extra $900 million in the la st Budget alone that was targeted for
vulnerable children and their families. I am very proud of what this Government has
actually provided for New Zealanders in the last 5 years of being in Government. This
is a very different picture from when voter s elected the National-led Government back
in 2008. The worst global financial crisis had struck New Zealand, and New Zealand
was already in recession. Treas ury advice signalled that we would be in Budget deficits
and increasing debt for a ver y, very long time. The debt projection was actually $150
billion and the current debt projection is ar ound $50 billion. That is  like cutting $100
billion off the debt—not million but billion. If  you look at it in a family situation,
imagine that a family has a $150,000 mortgage and they work really , really hard to
reduce the mortgage debt down to $50,000. That difference will make a humungous
difference to the family and what they ca n do as a family a nd the budget that they
actually have. That is what this Governme nt has delivered for New Zealand: $100
billion off our debt. That, I have to say, is an amazing out come that this Government
has delivered for New Zealanders.
This Government is focused on growing our economy to provide more jobs and
rising incomes, to provide a positive result for New Zealand. But many families and
businesses are still finding it quite difficu lt. I know. I have heard from even my
community, from people within the ethnic co mmunities, that often they are the ones
who are, in fact, struggling because they come from other countries, often they do not
speak the English language, and they find it difficult to get into careers or jobs that they
were used to in their home countries. Yet th ey actually celebrate th e fact that they are
living in this country, which is very gener ous compared with where they come from.
We provide for New Zealanders. On average, wages are increasing faster than inflation,
and business confidence is at its highest level in 20 years.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Well, look, after that speech from the member Melissa
Lee, I think we need to put the record stra ight a little. We absolutely need to put the
record straight, because it was under Labour that we had the lowest unemployment rate
16290 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
for a very, very long time in this countr y. It was under Labour. Remember this: under a
Labour Government we had the first or seco nd lowest rate of unemployment in the
OECD, but under this Government that has sl umped to about eighth or ninth place the
last time I looked. New Zealand is probably down to about 12 th place now in the OECD
for unemployment numbers. Why is that import ant? What that tells us is that every
single one of those OECD countries went th rough the global financial crisis. Not many
of them were in the privileged position that New Zealand was in because of the
surpluses that the Labour G overnment saved up over 9 year s. Over 9 years in every
single year there was a surplus, and that m eant that New Zealand was in a much better
position than almost any other OECD country  when it came to dealing with the global
financial crisis and when it came to dealing with unemployment.
What has this Government done—what has it done? New Zealand has slumped in the
OECD when it comes to the number and th e proportion of unemployed in our society.
Government members celebrate that—they celebrate that. Melissa Lee and the Hon
Paula Bennett think that they have done a fabulous job. Well, if they looked at the
international community and they looked at  what they were given on a plate—on a
plate—from the Labour Government, then they  would know that they have failed. They
have absolutely failed.

items.speaker: Hon Jo Goodhew
items.text: Oh, what a mess we were given—10 years of deficits.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Jo Goodhew can yell and scream as much as she likes, but the
facts speak for themselves. Go, Mrs Goodhew, and look at the OECD ratings. We were
the first or second in the ratings under the Labour Government, and we have now
slumped. We have now slumped. So that is th e record of this Government, and no one
should be confused about that.
The other record of this Government is that not only has it ha d a very poor track
record in terms of actually bringing down th e number of unemployed during the global
financial crisis but it has miscalculated and made its policy decisions for the last 4 years
on false figures—on false figures—from Treasury. The Treasury figures—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: That’s right. I think it was deliberate.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: —I think it is deliberate, Mr  Little; I agree with that—have
confused the whole picture, so that 20,000 children living  in poverty were not being
counted by this Government. No wonder it s policies are wrong. No wonder it has not
worked out that the way to address child pove rty is to actually in crease the financial
resources of those families. That is the an swer to it. Fiddling around with immunisation
is not going to actually addre ss the issue of the financial problems and the crises that
those families find themselves in.

items.speaker: Hon Jo Goodhew
items.text: Don’t you call saving lives fiddling.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Jo Goodhew may yell and scream about it, but that  is still not
going to get one more cent into those familie s where they actually need to be able to
provide food, provide decent shelter, and provide the necessitie s of life for their
children. I think it is a di sgrace that we have 285,000 ch ildren in poverty in New
Zealand—and the number is growing; every ti me Treasury revises its figures, it is
growing—because this is the land of milk a nd honey. We are not one of those countries
without resources. We are not one of those countries without the means to get by. We
are a South Pacific country with everything going for it.
Well, we did have everything going for us  when we had a Government that had a
plan in place, a Government that cared a bout addressing inequali ty, and a Government
that brought in the Working for Families package. That party opposite called it
communism by stealth, but that package brough t the largest number of children out of
poverty that we have ever seen  in recent times in this co untry. On this side of the
Chamber we are deeply proud of that, because  that is the practic al way of actually
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16291
addressing issues that matter to families—th e real issues. They are not the trumped-up
issues, not the trumped-up figures from Treasury, and not the diversion that the
Government seems keen on, pointing fingers  at members over on this side of the
Chamber. The Government needs to actually address the very real issues that its policies
are creating for everyday New Zealanders ever y day of the week. As for the assertion
that the Government is somehow getting all th is number of New Zealanders into work,
it is not.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is always interestin g to listen to chardonnay
socialists talking about the w hole aspect of poverty, because the thing is that for all the
talk, I would like to see where the action is . Mrs Moroney talked about a proud record
under the Labour Government. What she forgot to do is continue to  read the Salvation
Army report of 2008. This is what it clearly says. This is this proud record that she talks
about. It says that the social outcomes ach ieved over the previous 5 years, under the
previous Labour-led Government, were “s omewhat mixed and in some areas quite
disappointing.” That is the record that that member talks about.
Chardonnay socialists talk about the issue of  poverty, but my concern is that they do
not know what true poverty is and how to work with a comm unity to be able to solve
those issues. The Salvation Army noted that “M ore of our children appear to be at risk
of harm, more of our young people are engaged in petty crime, there is more violent
crime and more people in our jails.” Again, that is the record that the member just talked
about. The Salvation Army talked about  how, overall, New Zealanders were
“chronically indebted” and that “home ownership rates have fallen.” That is the Labour
Government of 9 years, which was in surplus and had much to give, yet with all that it
had, with as much money as it had, it still could not solve the social issues that are there.
The report continues. I know that Labour me mbers do not like to hear it. They have
gone quiet on the other side. Iain Lees-Galloway is yawning. Why? Because he does not
like to hear the truth. Here is more of the tr uth. The report lists the billions and billions
of taxpayer dollars that had been spent and yet concluded that this spending “seems to
have contributed very little to [New Zealand’ s] social progress.” So  if you ar e going to
use the report, if you are going to  use it as a basis to found y our ideals, then do read its
history. Read its history. That is what it is saying.
In fact, it says that many indicators were going backwards in 2008. There were rising
numbers of referrals to Child, Youth and Family and more children in Child, Youth and
Family care. There was rising youth offending.  For all the talk and all the rhetoric,
Labour members are just a bunch of chardonnay socialists talking about things but not
getting on with action. This is a Government and a Minister for Social Development
who are getting on with the action.

items.speaker: Let us talk about rheumatic fever prevention
items.text: $21.3 million—that is the figure. I was
honoured to be with the honourable Minister  of Health, Tony Ryall. We were at
Finlayson Park School—the largest primar y school in the whole of New Zealand,
predominantly M āori and Pacific children—with the 800 kids who are there. We
launched the Rheumatic Fever Prevention Pr ogramme. Parents came along. This is not
just about talk; this is about action. That is what this Government is actually about.
Let us talk about early childhood education, its expansion, and the targeted approach.
There is $172 million in total early childhood ed ucation investment. We know that it is
really important to deal not only with the health issues when we talk about poverty.
What about the educational needs of our ch ildren? There are a num ber of our children
who need to be engaged. Do you want to know what the percentage of early childhood
education engagement and participation was under the Labour Govern ment of 9 years?
It was 65 percent—65 percent. If you want to  talk about what is shameful, that is
shameful. What is it under the National-led G overnment, a Government of action? It is
16292 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
88 percent—that is what we have got—and cl imbing. So we are seeing the investment
in our children as absolutely important as  well. There are 700 more children in high
need—with $9.3 million announced from current funding, from the Targeted Assistance
for Participation Fund that is there.
Let us talk about kin carers and grandparents raising grandchildren.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Come and stand in Te Atatū.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: There is $35 million of additional funding, Mr Twyford. There
is financial help and a refere nce group to decide how best to spend this. Let us talk
about what is needed for the kids, Mr Tw yford. You can have all the talk and the
rhetoric and it is all just talk. He is another chardonna y socialist who grew up in
Ponsonby and somehow managed to go to the pe ninsula. But when we talk about what
happened to the children over those 9 years, there is no thing—nothing. That is what
happened, OK?
Let us talk about what we  are doing. Microfinancing—the  Government is exploring
with banks and NGOs alternatives to loan sh arks for low-income earners. You see, we
know where the risks are and we are actually doing pragmatic and practical things to
address them. What about housing insulation?  More bedrooms, more homes, more land
supply, warrants of fitness, $100 million to expand home insulati on targeted at low-
income families—you see, I am just going to keep going right the way through. You are
going to love this. Why? B ecause it is not just rhetoric and it is not just
“chardonnayism”—

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Chardonnayism!

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: —it is action that is actu ally happening on the ground. I know
that Mr Prasad loves to h ear this: 3,000 new State house bedrooms, 500 new homes, a
warrant of fitness trial to start with Housing New Zealand homes. We know that the
issue around having affordable housing and ac cessible housing is absolutely critically
important to our families as well.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I just want to thank
the speakers who have sat down. What they have  pointed out is someth ing that is really
important. Is it not interesting, though, that  what we have not had from the Labour
members is a discussion on welfare? This is  supposedly Labour’s hot topic. This is
supposedly where it holds the Government to  account. It is supposedly our weakness.
The reality is that we have 17,000 fewer New Zealanders on benefits today than we did
12 months ago. Do you know how many childre n that is? That is 12,000 fewer children
living in benefit-dependent households.
Do you know what this Government’s legacy is? It is nearly $500 million more spent
on support for welfare. That means 354 more  front-line staff who are working with
people. That means that where we used to see around 10,000 people face to face, we
now see more than 100,000 people face to face. That means we call them in and we talk
to them about what they can do, not what they cannot. We talk a bout the trai ning that
will support them into jobs. We then put real  money behind them, which then sees them
going into jobs.
What we see is that more than 8,000 sole parents have themselves gone into work.
What I hear from those sole parents who come  up to me is: “I have to admit, I never
thought I would be thanking you, but that was the first time someone asked me what I
wanted to do, what I could do, and what suppor t I needed for that to actually happen.”
That means real support like aiding people to get a driver’s  licence. It means helping
them with their CVs. And, yes, it means he lping them gain confidence, because more
often than not, if you have been out of work for a long time, if you live in a family that
has not worked, then actually having that c onfidence to put yourself  out there is huge.
The difference between this National Govern ment and what you have heard from the
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16293
Opposition tonight is that we celebrate thei r success. We believe in them and their
capabilities. With the right s upport at the right time, they can  make a difference in their
lives.
So we talk about poverty, and we certainly have the Opposition raising it as their sort
of topic. What the Opposition does not talk about, because they might be dirty words,
are parental responsibilities and families actua lly stepping in and helping each other,
and the fact that it takes a community and, yes, it takes Government support as well.
Actually, that sort of backing without put ting the right support in—throwing money at
them and hoping—was what we saw in the 2000s, and it did not make a difference to
those people who needed it most. It is ha rd, complex work that needs wraparound
support to lead people to independence. That  is the difference for families that are
struggling in New Zealand.
We do that through the Children’s Action Plan, because we see some our most
vulnerable children not able to access the kinds of services and help that they need—and
it is not all about Government; more often it is more about how they can help
themselves. More often than not it is role m odelling that shows them there is a different
way in life. More often than not it is access to  that health care that they need and access
to education for their children.
While we are at it, we will talk about education, because without a doubt getting
those children into early childhood education and seeing them stay in school longer will
hold the biggest difference. We have seen a huge reduction—a 30 percent reduction—in
teen pregnancies and teen births in this country. That is something to celebrate. I myself
go around every teen parent unit I can and meet  every teen parent I can. Do you know
what the best thing is, I thi nk, about being a teen mum, and I was one myself? It is that
you get to love your children longer. If you have them earlier, you actually get to have
them for a bit longer and you get to love them a bit longer.
But you know what those girls can do? They sit in front of me and I say to them “So,
why are you here? Why are you in education?”,  and they will go “Oh, because you told
us we had to, because we couldn’t get the benefit without it, because we’ve got to create
a better future for ourselves.” Every single determinant, every research you look at, and
every evaluation report will tell you how we know those children will do well. The one
determinant that will make the biggest difference for those kids is their mums. Their
mother’s educational achievement, whether they have got work experience, and how
solid their relationship is are the best things  we can do for those kids. So what are we
going to do? More than $40 million is going into  childcare so that that mum can be in
some form of education. We actually set some responsibi lities for them. We expect
them to be in education if they want a bene fit. We expect them to do budgeting courses.
We expect them to do parenting courses. And we are making a difference.
Report noted.
Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade

Department of Corrections

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I want to tell the Committee about what is
probably a very topical aspect of correc tions, which the Law and Order Committee saw
for itself last Friday on a trip to Auckland. It was a combined visit, having a look at
policing and corrections in Au ckland. If I am to focus dow n on corrections, it is a good
story to tell because we did tw o visits to correcti ons facilities. The fi rst one was to the
women’s prison at Wiri. What was most notable for the committee was that this was a
16294 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
visit to a working prison, so the focus on rehabilitation is extr emely strong in the
women’s prison at Wiri. Most of the women—I think it wa s in the high 90s—are doing
something like 40 hours’ work per week, and that  is to prepare them for their release.
We know they are going to be released, so the 40 hours of work is to prepare them for
that.
The committee, made up of cross-party membership—the Greens, New Zealand
First, Labour, and National—had a good tour  around Wiri, and we went into two or
three different real work situations. The fi rst one was into the kitchens, where we saw
the women preparing meals as if they were  in a real commercial kitchen. That was
because if you are not going to teach them what a real commercial kitchen is like, if you
are going to wrap them in prison cotton wool, then you are not going to show them what
the real work environment is like on the outside. The gentleman who was the supervisor
has worked extensively in the private sector  in hospitality, and he was very proud of
what his inmates were achieving. So we looke d in the kitchen, and not only were they
preparing every meal for the inmates but they were also doing all the meals and
manning the canteen for the workforce for the men’s prison construction at Wiri Prison.
I was pretty impressed, actually, when I walked into that commercial kitchen and
saw not only the women measuring out how ever many grams the prisoner allowance
was for the women in the women’s prison but also making things like pizza and panini
to be sold in the canteen for the workfor ce that was building the men’s prison. So they
were learning things like, obviously, how to prepare food, how to budget, provisioning,
and all those skills surrounding working in a commercial kitchen. They were operating
the kitchen within the confines of being w ithin a prison, but pretty  much in line with
what they would find in the outside world. It seemed to me that the women prisoners in
that environment were not only enjoying themselves, but clearly they were learning new
skills. There were a couple of women there making muffins to go on sale the next day.
There were, as I say, pizzas and panini and hot chips, and all those things that get sold
in a shop catering for workers.
We then went into the distribution centre, and, again, there are a lot of skills involved
in distribution centres. Think about EziBuy and the huge distributi on centre there, or
think about any supermarket chain and the distribution network needed there. What
blew me away about that portion of th e visit was that the women were getting
qualifications in running forklifts. I said : “Oh, crikey, how ma ny men have forklift
skills and qualifications?”. Well, it is mo stly men. I said: “OK,  how many women?”.
Hardly any. Well, hello, there will be a number of women leaving the prison system
who are qualified to run forklifts.
I met in particular two women, and I do not recall their name s. One woman said:
“Look, I know I’ve made mistakes.” She was convicted for fraud. Sh e said: “I got out
on parole. I went back to wh ere I came from. I was str uggling, I didn’t have enough
money, and my kids needed stuff. I was back in my old environment and I went back to
what I knew, which was fraud.” She got caught, she is back in prison, and she is saying:
“Look, these skills I’m learning now, I want to  use them so that when I do go back out
on parole”—and she will go back out on parole—

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Can I start tonight by
congratulating the magnificent staff of corrections, who have worked professionally and
enthusiastically and in a dedicated manner fo r the financial year that we are currently
reviewing. We are lucky in this country to  have such a profe ssional staff manning our
prisons and looking after the 34,000 to 35,000 people who are serving community
sentences.
As the previous speaker, Jacqui Dean, sai d, there is a lot happening in our prisons
and with those who are serving community se ntences. This Government has set them a
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16295
target of reducing reoffending by 25 percen t by the year 2017. Reporting against the
Better Public Services target at September of last year, we ha d reached 11.4 percent.
The current figure stands at about 11.7 percent.  That is as a result of some outstanding
work from our staff. So, yes, we have incr eased the amount of edu cation that is being
made available to those who are serving sentences in our prisons and those who are
serving community sentences.
Every person now who enters a New Zeala nd prison gets an educational assessment
and has developed for them an educational pl an. They are getting skills training, they
are getting on-the-job training, as we have just heard fr om Jacqui Dean. They are
getting drug and alcohol rehabilitation, and that has certainly ramped up. We have three
working prisons. They are structured around a normal 40-hour week that includes both
work and qualification and skills training. Th e three youth prisons that we have also
have a 40-hour work week but it is based around education and gaining qualifications.
A number of outstanding things have ha ppened throughout the la st financial year.
One of them that I would like to mention picks up on the previous speaker, Jacqui Dean,
talking about working in a commercial kitchen. That is fantastic, and they are learning
extremely good skills and doing a great job. Rimuta ka Prison in this last year took part
in Visa Wellington on a Plate. Martin Bosley, the chef, went and worked with some of
the prison cooks and then delivered to the public a restaurant-quality  meal as part of
Visa Wellington on a Plate. It was the fastest-selling offering from Visa Wellington on a
Plate, and the organisers have come back ag ain this year wanting the prison to continue
with this. One of the staff was actually  taken on immediately and worked in a
commercial kitchen. The skills that both the waiters and the cooks learnt will stand them
in very good stead, I am sure.
I just want to pick up on an area that is given a lot of prominence from time to time,
mainly from a critical point of view, and that is around prisoner health. Just today I got
the latest magazine from the Department of  Corrections, which focuses on health. I just
want very quickly to take this opportunity to talk about a couple of things that are
happening that have not perhaps had the prom inence they deserve. First of all, this
Government has opened a High Dependency Unit  in a prison—20 beds initially, mainly
for dementia patients, because, like the general population, the prison population is
ageing. We have over 100 pr isoners who are aged over 70, and we are now expanding
that unit by another 10 beds. It has been extremely successful.
At Auckland Region Women’s Corrections Facility the health service has now taken
on board the fact that it is a working pris on and the women are working a structured 40-
hour week. They do not want to take time off work to go and visit the nursing staff, so
the nursing staff have now made themselves available 7 days a week. They are making
themselves available around the normal work hours for those women. It is a fantastic
partnership approach to health. Wh ānau Ora visits on a re gular basis now in the
Northland prison, and it visits during regular visiting times so that it can work with the
families who are visiting prisoners. They ar e generally hard-to-reach people, and it
knows they regularly visit their family members in that jail. That is a very good time for
Whānau Ora to be talking to them. I could go on for much longer.
Report noted.
New Zealand Police

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The Police too have had an outstanding
year. This country is well served by its over 12,000 Police employees, and, again, I
want to take this opportunity to thank them for all their hard work throughout the year
and to congratulate them on the results they ar e getting in keeping this country safe and
protecting our communities. We have seen over the last 3 years a continual reduction in
16296 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
recorded crime, totalling a 17.4 percent reduction in recorded crime. That is a 33-year
low. That is the proof of the work the poli ce are doing. I know that there are people in
this Chamber who hark back to the good old days; actually, policing is now a very
technologically based service. It uses  good information. Our police are the best
equipped they have ever been and they are looking after our communities and keeping
them safe in all sorts of different ways that perhaps were not even dreamt of 5 or 6 years
ago. I want to touch on just a couple.
There are 34 neighbourhood policing teams acr oss the country. They are working in
our most vulnerable communities. These are places where we see huge amounts of
crime committed again and again and again ag ainst the same victims. They are focused
on those communities that are continually revi ctimised by a small number of criminals.
They are working with each of those communities to find ways to address the drivers of
crime. In some parts it is about drugs and alcohol—there is no doubt about that. In some
of the other parts I have visited, teams have  talked about a very common problem being
the lack of access to supermarkets. People had to do all their shopping at a grocery
store, where everything is much more e xpensive and their money was not going far
enough, so transport—community vans, mobile vans, etc.—was made available to take
people to the shops. There is a whole raft of things: getting rid of graffiti, working with
people to keep their houses safe, etc.
As for boy racer offences, I announced not long ago that we have seen them
halved—halved—in the time since we introduced that piece of legisl ation. That is not
about catching young people and crushing their cars. That is about keeping communities
safe, both from the nuisance value those boy ra cers create in the co mmunities they tear
around and also from the harm to some of  the innocent bystanders and the innocent
passengers, who have been killed or maimed by the excessive speeds seen from these
boy racers. We have seen deaths of 15 to  24-year-olds drop down from 105 when we
introduced the legislation to 66.
I also announced an increase in foot patr ols. This is about having the police much
more visible out in our communities where they can prevent crime happening. There has
been an increase over the last  couple of years in the numbe r of foot patrols by 155. In
2011 they had just on 41,000 foot patrols;  in 2013 they had 104,000. When I go around
New Zealand and talk to people about safety in their communities, the first thing people
say to me is that the police are much more visible. They see them out on the streets,
walking around, talking to people, and keeping an eye on the hot spots.
The other thing I would say is about a programme called Turning the Tide. Very
quickly, this is working with iwi to address the drivers of crime in the M āori
community. We are seeing some enormous su ccesses. If I talk just about my own
electorate of East Coast a nd about Gisborne, the police have placed a policewoman
inside the r ūnanga of Ngati Porou. She is doing an outstanding job working with her
iwi, trying to prevent crime, trying to keep  people safe. She has got a fantastic garden
programme running with some of the gang me mbers at Kaiti. She has got them into
education, getting some skills and training, and the kids are at school—all sorts of
incredible things. These pe ople are working quietly on the ground, often unseen, out in
our communities. We are lucky to have such a fantastic police service, which is working
to keep New Zealanders safe.
Report noted.
Vote Housing, Non-departmental appropriations

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chairman. The first point I
want to make about funding for affordable housing is how woefu lly inadequate the
Social Housing Fund actually was, particularly when you consider the staggeringly high
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16297
need, and, secondly, how little of that woefully inadequate amount was actually spent
on housing.
I have got to highlight t hose figures here. Only $28 m illion was actually allocated
and only $16 million was spent. How bad is that? The Government takes only 2 days to
decide to spend $30 million on  Rio Tinto, but in a whole bloody year cannot spend $28
million on housing for the poor. How is that for poor performance? The Government
got only $28 million, but through bureaucratic inefficiency it managed to spend only
$16 million, and has delivered only 165 houses. What a shambles.
But that is not the worst part. The worst pa rt is that the Government’s policies are
leading to huge numbers of low-income families being evicted from their homes, State
houses being disposed of, and large tracts of  State housing land being sold off to make
way for high-end housing estates, because National believes that the private sector is the
best place to provide for housing. E hoa, ēhara tērā i te pūru tūtae noa iho.
[Friend, that’s simply just not bull’s droppings.]
There is nowhere in the world where the pr ivate sector provides quality, long-term,
affordable housing for the poor, and it certai nly ain’t happening here, where thousands
of families are forced to rent high-priced, damp, draughty, and cold flats, houses, and
caravans on the open market, because the State no longer wants to bother.
Those living in State houses are being s hunted out of them, as we speak—like the
family who have lived in a home in Glen Inne s for the past 33 years but are about to be
evicted by Housing New Zealand this Friday, as  part of the sale of State properties to
the private sector and the redevelopment of the area. Housing New Zealand says it is
evicting the family for alleged antisocial behaviour. Is it not funny how a family can
live in a house for 33 years without any major problems but the minute that mum speaks
out against policies that have led to the eviction of friends and neighbours whom her
family has known for decades, all of a sudden her family are being evicted for antisocial
behaviour? Betty has lived in Glen Innes all her life. She is  a postal worker, a cleaner, a
member of the Amalgamated Engineeri ng, Printing and Manufacturing Union, and a
regular volunteer at the Glen Innes Primary School.
Late last year Betty’s sister’s family were evicted from the home where their family
had lived for 54 years. Betty herself has just  come out of hospital, where she underwent
a procedure for breast cancer. She is tired, she is unwell, and now , thanks to these
Housing New Zealand policies, she is about to become homeless. Betty’s family want to
stay in their home and fight the eviction, an d the public are invite d to support them by
marching with her this Thursday at 6 p.m. on Taniwha Street in Glen Innes.
The housing crisis in low socio-ec onomic areas like Glen Innes, P ōmare, and
Maraenui has actually been worsened by H ousing New Zealand policies that demonise
poor families and devastate communities, leaving empty houses and unsafe
neighbourhoods. If that was not enough, the Go vernment is now reviewing all tenancies
and shifting the allocation of State housing from Housing New Zealand to Work and
Income New Zealand, bringing even greater  insecurity and evermore bureaucratic
harassment for low-income families. That is not a future that any Government should be
seeking.
The Government should, instead, take a positive approach to the problem by
engaging in a comprehensive programme of building 10,000 new State houses every
year for at least the next 5 years, to help address the critical shortage of healthy homes
for low-income families and because building homes does more than just provide
houses for people. It creates thousands of jobs in design, architecture, carpentry,
cabinetmaking, community infrastructure, and all the related jobs that come with a
strong and vibrant housing sector. It helps to build healthy families and healthy
communities, because when people are working everybody is happy.
16298 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
I have no doubt that a Government-funded home-building programme would be well
received by local bodies and by iwi, both of whom have a h uge interest in seeing their
communities engaged in meaningful work and who would happily come to the party on
consent issues and availabil ity of land for housing developm ent. There is no question
that we do have a housing crisis, but we also have the ability to deal with it quickly and
positively. All it takes is the political will to do so. Kia ora.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I want to acknowledge Mr  Hone Harawira and his
comments, especially around Glen Innes. I want to talk about Glen Innes because I have
lived in a home in the area for the last 18 years. I know the people well and the
community well. I know the struggles and I know the issues that he talked about.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: You’re not very popular there now.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I am, Mr Twyford, actually. The f act is that we have worked
quite hard there for quite a long time. T āmaki Transformation, which came under the
Labour Government, started to look at a w hole-of-community perspective, and housing
was one of those issues. Out of  that issue we worked collectively with the Government
agency, a whole community working together, to address these issues.
But here is one of the shameful things th at the Labour Government needs to be held
to account for. It had some of the worst housing stock in the whole of New Zealand.
Fifty-eight percent of that area, the communi ties of Glen Innes, Panmure, and Point
England, was State housing stock. It had some of the worst stock. In other words, under
that Government’s watch there was a lack of maintenance and there was a lack of repair.
In other words, there was a lack of concer n—there was a lack of  concern. For all the
talk, let us talk about the action, and let us  talk about the reality. Nothing was done over
9 years in those very communities. I can ta ke you to the streets. Flanders Street—we
can go up there—and Ropata Avenue. We can name the streets. I am not sure that Mr
Twyford can name the streets, but we can name the streets where the homes and the
houses that these families had to live in were  really shameful. If you want to talk about
Government responsibility, that was shameful.
So what did this Government decide to do? This is what it decided to do. It was time
for change. Inside of that change, yes, there were diffi culties and struggles because
some of those families had been there for such a long time. But I can say this. A number
of the community initiatives are there, even  at the moment. There is an organisation
called Ng ā Iwi Katoa, which Monte Cecilia Hous ing Trust is involved in with David
Zussman, and there is a collective of the community working together with the T āmaki
Redevelopment Company to try to address some of the critical concer ns that are there.
This is what we are doing as a Government to address them. There have been 6,960 new
tenancies started and 200,000 people in our houses. But I want to talk about some other
things. When they were asked and surveyed, right across the board, with regard to how
they found the service and what it was doing, yes, there were some areas of need, but 76
percent of those surveyed were satisfied wi th their house maintenance and the customer
services centre. That was not the figure under a Labour Government of 9 years. That
was not the figure that was there.
Hone talked about the importance of ha ving healthy housing a nd home insulation.
One of the things we have had over th is period of time is 2,000 whole-of-house
upgrades. We have spent $190 million to improve the quality of our houses. You see,
again, this is a Government of  action, not just of talk. This  is a Government that has
made a difference to those homes. We have insulated 8,295 homes. In other words, we
are making a difference to the care and concern of the families—even those families
that are in Glen Innes. There have b een 390,000 maintenance actions. We know, again,
that the maintenance of, and repairs to, a number of those homes was quite critical to
our families.
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16299
I also want to talk abou t social housing and the whol e thing around the third-tier
sector—the third sector of the housing market that is out there. I can say this. We know
that Brian Donnelly, for instance, of the New Zealand Housing Foundation, the
Salvation Army, the Monte Cecilia Housing Tr ust, and a number of these collectives
have come together and said that this is the right intent, this is a good initiative, and they
want to see the ability to come in to that se ctor to truly make a difference. Here is the
difference that they can make. They can make a difference because they can meet the
needs of those housing issues for their communities in particular. So there is $2.9 billion
for housing, to add bedrooms to 3,000 homes, to build 500 new homes, and to complete
home insulations and repairs inside our Housing New Zealand stock.
That is the difference that this Governme nt is making. We are now starting to hear
families that are saying: “Now not only do we have healthy homes but we can access
things like health services and education.” There has been a concer n about some of our
families, even in Glen Innes. We had the petition for P ōmare and Maraenui as well.
What we know is this. I want to comme nd the new Chief Executive of Housing New
Zealand, Glen Sowry, who even in his firs t month went and visited the homes. He
visited them with the case managers to se e what was actually happening on the ground,
and saw how it was making a difference. Here is the difference. Mr Chris Hipkins was
in Maraenui about 2 or 3 weeks ago, and he celebrated the success of what was
happening. They were making a difference, to address the issues—

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I want to address the question of why this
National Government has so completely failed to address the housing crisis. I think that
is the interesting question. Everybody knows that there is a housing crisis. It is affecting
first home buyers. It is affecting State house tenants. Government agencies are routinely
referring people to live in campgrounds. There are 285,000 children growing up in cold,
damp homes, and who are constantly sick because of the state of our housing stock. The
country knows that there is a housing crisis. The National Party knows that there is a
housing crisis. That is why Nick Smith runs  around like a jack-in-the-box every 2 days.
He would turn up to the opening of a door handle. He has got some half-baked scheme
he announces every couple of days, like th e one where he was flogging off broken-
down old State houses in parts of the country  where there is no housing crisis. He was
flogging them off at knock-down rates to make it look as if he is  doing something. We
know that there is a housing crisis. The National Party knows it. But why has it not done
anything about it? That is the interesting question, and that is what I want to address.
Let us take the issue of these loan-to-valu e ratio lending restrict ions. They have had
the effect of locking out a generation of  young New Zealanders from the dream of
homeownership. Over the last week I have visited a number of cities around the North
Island, and some of those plac es are cities where first home  buyers have been the worst
affected in New Zealand by loan-to-value ratio lending restrictions. I am talking
particularly about Napier, Wanganui, and Palmerston North.  These are places where
first home buyers have basically had the draw bridge pulled up. They have been told to
go away—do not bother, do not come back; you are not going to be  able to buy your
own home.
I met a young family in Hamilton. They had moved from Auckland to avoid
Auckland’s high property prices. They were a young couple with kids. They moved to
Hamilton to avoid the skyrocke ting house prices in Auckland. They told me that now,
because of loan-to-value ratio restrictions that have been broadened by this Government
and because of the 20 percent minimum deposits, they are 3 years away from being able
to summon up a deposit. This is a family with professional, well-paid jobs, so imagine
the stretched lower-middle and middle income people, who believe th at they should be
able to own their own home. They are utterly locked out.
16300 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
Let us look at healthy homes. The Minist er of Housing announced the other day a
pilot scheme—he re-announced last yea r’s Budget commitment—involving 500 State
houses to see whether the Government could make a warrant of fitness scheme work.
The State houses are all already insulated. Th ey have been retrof itted and insulated.
They do not need a warrant of fitness pilot sc heme. What they need is for the Minister
to pick up the phone and tell the chief execu tive of Housing New Zealand that he wants
those houses built to a certain standard so th at they are warm and dry. So instead of
doing the thing that is necessary—tackling co ld, damp homes in the private rental
sector—this Minister is doing more busywork with a trial warrant of fitness with his
own State houses.
The third example of this Government’s tota l failure to address the housing crisis is
its mismanagement and incompetent neglect of  the State housing asset. We currently
have 4,000 empty State houses in New Zealand—4,000. By coincidence, there are about
4,000 people languishing on the waiting lists, and that is after Phil Heatley narrowed the
eligibility criteria so tightly that hardly  anybody these days qualifies to get a State
house. In the last 12 months  the number of State houses in New Zealand has decreased
by 700. Under this National Government there are fewer State houses than ever before.
Iain Lees-Galloway and I were in Palmer ston North last week. We visited Highbury
in Palmerston North. Palmerston North has about 90 vacant State houses. In Highbury
they are boarded up, they are covered in gr affiti, and they are a magnet for vandalism
and crime. Such is the neglect of the Stat e housing. It is the si ngle most valuable
publicly owned asset. We have $46 billio n worth of State hous ing, and all over New
Zealand, in every provincial city, you can s ee them rotting, boarded up, and covered in
graffiti. This Government has brought dow ntown Detroit to Napier, to Palmerston
North, to Hamilton, to Gisborne, to Wanganui—you name it.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: It is probably worthwhile doing a
timely comparison between the Labour Party’ s record on housing when in Government
and what has happened under the current Gove rnment. Nothing would be more apt than
to remind New Zealanders of interest ra tes under the Labour Government from 1999 to
2008. People will recall that during those heady years of Helen Clark and that big-
spending Government, interest rates for firs t-home buyers were ar ound 8 percent, or 9
percent, or 10 percent per annum. That is right.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: Up to 11 percent.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: First-home buyers who are listening to this speech today
will sit and wonder how they would ever cope if a Labour  Government came in and
started running mortgage interest rates at 8 percent or 9 percent. I stand corrected by the
member for Waitaki, Jacqui Dean, who reminds  me that, actually, interest rates hit 11
percent under the Helen Clark Government . I do apologise—under the previous Labour
Government mortgage interest rates for fi rst-home buyers were around 9 percent, 10
percent , and 11 percen t. Under the National Government we have seen interest rates
oscillate at around 5 percent and 6 percent. They may go as high as 7 percent, but not
the dizzying target of the big-spending Labour Government of 11 percent, I am sure. So
there you have mortgage interest rates—a housing issue for all who borrow to buy a
home, which is usually everyone.
The second comparison would be those hous es in Highbury and ot her parts of the
country where the Labour Government allo wed gangs and gang members to run rife,
not just in State housing but  in State housing neighbourhoods. It allowed scams to
occur, such as subletting. It allowed people to undertak e violent behaviour—picking up
glass and the pickets from the picket fen ces and beating up their neighbours—and did
not do a single thing about it in State housing neighbo urhoods. Today we see the
statistics where up to 400 St ate house tenants have been m oved on in the last few years
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16301
because of their violent, dysfunctional, and antisocial behaviour in State housing
neighbourhoods. The Labour Party members have  gone quiet on the other side of the
Chamber because they know that they neve r dealt with those problems in State housing
neighbourhoods, but the National Government has.
The third issue is the insulation of State houses. I would be very proud if I was Nick
Smith for being the Minister of Housing who oversaw the insulation of every single
State house in New Zealand that could be insulated. How is it that the Labour Party
after 9 years of Government left not thousa nds but tens of thousands of State houses
uninsulated? State houses were old, col d, and mouldy under the previous Labour
Government for almost a decade. Why has the barracking stopped? Why are the Labour
Party members no longer heckling me in the Chamber? They go quiet in shame.
Congratulations to Nick Smith on insula ting every single Stat e house across New
Zealand that could be insulated.
That brings me to the warrant of fitn ess. Nick Smith is introducing a Housing
Warrant of Fitness trial for States houses  across New Zealand. The Labour Government
never did it. Do you know why? Because its State houses would never pass a warrant of
fitness. The idea that the Labour Party woul d introduce some sort of warrant or housing
standard for private sector landlords—becau se this is what the Labour Party waxes
lyrical about: private sector  landlords across New Zealand needing to up their game.
The fact of the matter is that while in Government the Labour Party could not even
insulate or provide State houses of good quality  in its own stock, let alone in the private
sector’s. It never introduced a warrant of fitness because it could not even meet that
standard in State housing and it could not do it in the private sector area.
Fifthly, of course, the Labour  Party when in Government , with its legislation and
regulation, prevented land being supplied acr oss New Zealand in the provinces and the
metropolitan areas so that houses could be built. In fact, under that—

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I was not going to take
a call, but there has been some  misinformation that I felt needed to be cleared up. I am
an Associate Minister of Housing and the Mi nister for Social Development. Yes, there
are some changes going on w ith how we work with thos e who need houses, how we
work with the waiting list, how we get people into homes, and how we look at
reviewable tenancies and at  who is in our houses and who should be looking at
alternative options so that we can free up some of those houses . I agree with all
members of the House that we have some pe ople living in situations that none of us
would wish on anyone, quite frankly. To do this  we need those who are most in need
actually living in homes. So since 2011 we have advised people who are going into
Housing New Zealand houses that those hous es were not necessarily a house for life
and that we could be looking at some of the need as we went forward.
There are big changes happening on 14 April. We have certainly made them public
but I am not sure that they ar e getting the kind of attenti on that they perhaps should be.
No longer will Housing New Zealand place people into homes. That will be the
responsibility of Work and In come, and I think that is re ally important for the well-
being of those people. Mr Hara wira raised concerns about th at and felt that it would be
marginalising people. In fact , it is the complete opposite. Th e reality is that we know a
lot about people who are on benefits. We know how many children they have, we know
what their income is, we know what their ne eds will be longer term, and we know their
history of benefit receipt or with Child, Youth and Family. By taking all of those things
into consideration when we place someone in  a home, we can also be looking at the
wider social concerns.
So the reality is that if we set someone up in a home, their ch ildren are engaged in
school. We have the right kind of support going in to them, whether it be via an NGO, a
16302 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
programme like Family Start or Parents as  First Teachers, or one of those great
programmes that works with them. We keep them there for a very long time so that they
have that sense of community and are able  to stay engaged in work and schools.
However, there are some people who are payi ng market rent in a Housing New Zealand
home. That means that their income is such that they could actually afford, supposedly,
to be in a private rental. So th en it gets really interesting to look at what the barriers are
that are preventing them from going into a private rental. Quite often it can be bond
payments, quite often it can be fear, and qu ite often it can be just knowing what they
know. So we can actually put things in place that will assist people to overcome those
barriers so that we are freeing up homes for those most in need.
One of the other really importa nt things is, of course, th at we are opening it up to
social housing providers. So people like the Salvation Army, Vision West Community
Trust in my own patch out in west Auckla nd, and other organisations that actually do
engage in social housing will be able to access income-related rents, and that is massive
for them. That means that they can offer the tenants in their homes income-related rents,
which of course greatly reduces  the cost for the individual or family and, equally, also
makes it much easier for the organisation th at is supporting them, because they are no
longer reliant on just the accommodation supplement.
What you will see from 14 April is that we will have people on a waiting list that will
be going out to social housing providers as well as to Housing New Zealand. They will
be advising us on the homes that they have available. We will then be making the best
call for that individual or family as to wher e they live and what best suits their needs.
We then get far better wraparound support for th em. We get to identify what all of the
issues are. Although it is a massive change an d there is always some risk in how Work
and Income will handle that, with the increas e in staff for specialised services, I know
that we can make a really big difference. We will be making some announcements very
soon on reviewable tenancies. They will be sensible, they will be  common-sense, and
they will working alongside someone over a period of time. So someone is not going to
get notice of 1 month or even 2 months, or, for that matter,  even 3 months. We will be
working with them on what other opportuni ties there are and how we can place them
into homes. So I really welcome this.
I have heard other members raise the issu e of how many houses have been insulated.
I cannot even start to go on about the sp ecial housing areas in Auckland and the
difference they are making in homes being built and opening up ot her opportunities for
New Zealanders. This is a complex and a hard area, but it is one that I know National is
making a difference in, and Nick Smith deserves all recognition for the work that has
gone on.
Report noted.
Ministry for the Environment

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: The mission for the
Ministry for the Environment is environm ental stewardship for a prosperous New
Zealand, and I believe that it  is truly delivering on that goal, with three significant
environmental firsts in the last year. The ministry is strongly focused on improving New
Zealand’s freshwater management and it has led comprehensive reform in this area.
Based on the Land and Water Forum, whic h in itself was a real breakthrough in
terms of getting long-overdue action on wate r, the Ministry for the Environment has
developed the first ever National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management and now
a new national objectives framework for fresh water. This framework is scientifically
backed and will deliver real reform for freshwater management. It will support
communities to set freshwater objectives and water quality bottom lines to preserve our
4 Mar 2014 Financial Review Debate 16303
ecosystem and human health. I just want to not e that the numeric values that inform the
framework and bottom lines have been provid ed by over 60 freshwater scientists from
both the public and the private sectors and from academia. These values have been
tested against a reference group of water us ers, so they are practical and sensible
initiatives. The framework will provide a so lid platform for maintaining and improving
water quality in all our rivers, our lakes, and our wetlands. This is something that I think
all New Zealanders will support.
Another first for the ministry  is the work behind the Exclusive Economic Zone and
Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Act, which we passed last year. New Zealand
now, for the very first time, has a legisl ative framework to ensure environmental
protection for our oceans. This is essent ial regulation and is long overdue. Although
there has been an oil and gas industry opera ting in New Zealand waters for over 50
years, there has never been any protection, an d it is absolutely time to introduce that
now. This Act will protect our seas, and National has done it.
But probably the most influential first is th e work that the ministry has completed to
introduce the new Environmental Reporting Bill, which will come into the House later
this week. Without objective long-term mon itoring and reporting, it is impossible to
make scientifically valid and intelligent decisions about our environment. This bill will
provide comprehensive and independent repor ting, and that reporting will be analysed
by the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment. The reporting will be on the
domains of air, climate and atmosphere, fres h water, marine, and land, with an overlay
of biodiversity across all those areas. Finally we will have credible environmental
information to underpin our decisions. Too of ten in this Chamber we  debate the quality
of the information rather than the actions th at could make a significant difference to our
environment.
So I want to congratulate the Ministry fo r the Environment on the work that it has
done, as evidenced by these three firsts: th e national objectives framework for fresh
water, which will improve water quality across the country; the exclusive economic
zone legislation to protect our ocean environments; and the new environmental
reporting legislation, which will  provide scientifically base d information to influence
future environmental decision making. With these three firsts New Zealand has been
gaining a reputation for its innovative appr oach to bringing together successful
environmental and economic policy. That is  something that underpins National’s blue-
green philosophy, based on our belief that l ooking after the envi ronment and growing
our economy can, and must, go hand in hand fo r the long-term well-being of all New
Zealanders.
Report noted.
Ministry for Primary Industries
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labou r—West Coast - Tasman) : I will take just a
brief call. I refer members of the Committee to a Riddet Institute report that actually
outlines in a very clear way the importance of the area of respons ibility that the Hon
Nathan Guy and his department, his supe r-department, the Ministry for Primary
Industries, are responsible for, which is a very big part of our economy. And the fact
that it is leaderless is putting our whole economy at risk. To use the Minister’s own
words: “Biosecurity is my No. 1 priority.” Well, I appreciate that but we need more than
words to carry it through.
In the year gone past in th e biosecurity area the Minist er for Primary Industries has
let into New Zealand onion fly in garlic from China, palm  kernel expeller has finally
been identified as a high biosecurity risk, we  have got Psa in kiwifruit, we have got
Theileria running rampant through livestock in th e North Island, and we have got pork
16304 Financial Review Debate 4 Mar 2014
importation where his department took the por k industry to court, costing hundreds of
thousands of dollars, so that we could insist on getting pork from Canada into this
country, with huge risk. We have caught fr uit fly and we have got peach scale on
kiwifruit, and the Minister says that biosecurity is his No. 1 priority. If that is as good as
it gets, he has failed miserably and the department has as well.
Food safety is another crucia l area of the Ministry for Primary Industries. We have
had dicyandiamide because of a failure of oversight. We have had meat stuck on the
ports in China. We have had botulism because the Minister’s own Government
department AsureQuality failed to give good advice to his ministr y, the Ministry for
Primary Industries, and then failed to gi ve it to Fonterra—hundr eds of millions of
dollars of cost. And then with the meat e xports from this country, again, we have got
faecal contamination.
In every crucial area of our economy in the primary sector, oversight by the Ministry
for Primary Industries is failing—absolutely failing. The Government’s response is that
we will have Primary Growth Partnership funding—that is, a slush fund for its mates,
where $350 million of taxpayer funding has been  handed out for different projects. The
key performance indicators and the response on those projects are so bad that the Office
of the Auditor-General is currently investigating all the Primary Growth Partnership
grants. There are three areas—one where the Government is throwing money at its
mates; the other areas are biosecurity and food safety—where failure after failure is
occurring and putting our economy at risk.
What has happened in trade, another area under the supe r-ministry? Well, the last
good thing we had in trade was the responsib ility of my good friend and colleague the
Hon Phil Goff, and that was the free-trade ag reement with China. If it was not for him
and that deal, dare I say it, this economy would be on its knees.
So what has the National Government done? Well, it has tried to progress free-trade
agreements in a couple of different areas. Th e Trans-Pacific Partnership has failed. It
has stalled, and in spite of the Minister of Trade, the Hon Tim Groser, being overseas at
this moment pulling back from a free-trade agreement with Russia, which is not a bad
idea at the moment, I would suggest, he has shown no real progress in the area of trade.
So to come back to the area that we are talking about, the Ministry for Primary
Industries is an absolute failure in every area  of its core responsibil ities. In biosecurity
we are at serious risk, in food safety our reputation has slumped, and with the Primary
Growth Partnership I think the report of the Auditor-General that will come out in about
June, we think, will be incredibly revea ling and will expose the links between the
National Government, the National Party, a nd the people who have received funding
from this slush fund. In the area of trade, where there has always been some hope that
the Government is going to deliver for New Zealand, again, the Ministry for Primary
Industries has failed. The results are cuts for funding in this Government’s first Budget,
cuts to biosecurity, and merging a whole lot of responsibilities into one big super-
department to the point where even the i ndependent report on botulism said that the
core responsibilities of the Ministry for Primary Industries are being compromised.
